### Terraform Version

```shell
<= 1.13.1
```

### Use Cases

I love that [v1.5.x](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/releases/tag/v1.5.0) introduced the ability to surface messages during plan that are non-blocking (i.e. informational warnings).  This is _very helpful_ for module authors to be able to communicate with their consumers, e.g.
> don't use var.X anymore, it is now computed based on var.Y

I find the semantic very confusing, however, as it contains both the words **assert** and **error**, both of which have a strong connotation of a _blocking_ behavior

I learned [**assertions**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assertion_(software_development)) to be sanity checks that developers would add to communicate states that they assumed would be _impossible_.  If false, it meant a fundamental assumption no longer held and the code should stop executing immediately.  It is also a common semantic for failing a test case.

Similarly, I learned **errors** to be things that need an action (e.g. a build error requires a code change, an HTTP error requires a retry/request modification, or an unexpected/alternate code flow (e.g. in [go](https://go.dev/blog/error-handling-and-go))

### Proposal

Suggesting aliases (and maybe future deprecation for existing interface) to avoid using `assert` or `error`, perhaps:

```terraform
check "deprecated_vars" {
    warn {
        condition = var.instance_ami == null
        message   = "The variable 'instance_ami' is deprecated and should not be used."
    }
    warn {
        condition = var.override_instance_type == null
        message   = "The variable 'override_instance_type' is deprecated and should not be used."
    }
    # ...
}
```

this would also be open for extension to introduce a `error` `check` block.  that would have the same interface as `warn` but with plan-blocking behavior.  this would also make transitioning from a `warn` to an `error` an easy one (e.g. if sufficient time has been given for consumers to fix their warnings and we now want to force any stragglers)

#### `check` Semantics

existing | proposed
--- | ---
`assert` | `warn`
`error_message` | `message`
\- | `error`

#### Alternate Proposal

perhaps instead of `assert`, use `case`.  this could introduce a `block` list/set semantic (default to non-blocking, options for blocking plan and/or apply), e.g.

```terraform
    case {
        condition = var.instance_ami == null
        message   = "The variable 'instance_ami' is deprecated and should not be used."
        block     = [ plan ]
    }
```
issues.title: Warning semantics are confusing

### Terraform Version

```shell
v6.12.0
```

### Use Cases

In many real-world infrastructure projects, organizations maintain multiple Terraform repositories that rely on the same provider versions—especially when following a modular or microservices-based architecture. For example:

A company with 10+ Terraform repositories, each provisioning different AWS resources using the same version of the AWS provider (e.g., terraform-provider-aws v6.12.0).

Teams working on CI/CD pipelines where provider binaries are downloaded repeatedly across builds, wasting time and bandwidth.

Local development environments where multiple engineers have to re-download the same large provider binaries in each repo.

Currently, each repository independently downloads and stores the provider in its own .terraform directory. This leads to:

Redundant storage usage: e.g., the AWS provider binary (terraform-provider-aws_v6.12.0_x5) is approximately 740MB in size. With 10 repositories using the same version, that amounts to 7.4 GB of duplicated data.

Inefficient use of bandwidth: identical binaries are downloaded multiple times.

Increased setup time: repeated installation of the same provider version across repositories slows down initialization.

### Attempted Solutions

Some approaches we've considered or tried:

Symbolic Links: Attempted symlinking .terraform/providers across repos. However, this is error-prone and breaks Terraform’s internal dependency management, especially when dealing with checksums, dependency lock files (.terraform.lock.hcl), and version constraints.

Shared Terraform Plugin Cache (TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR): Terraform does offer a plugin cache via the TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR environment variable. While this helps reduce re-downloading, it does not prevent providers from being copied into each repo’s .terraform directory, thus failing to eliminate redundancy in disk space usage.


### Proposal

Introduce a centralized Terraform provider repository/cache directory, with shared usage across multiple Terraform projects on the same machine.

Key Features:

Centralized Provider Directory: Allow specifying a global path (e.g., ~/.terraform/providers/**) where Terraform can read and reference providers without duplicating them in each .terraform subdirectory.

Hard-link or Reference System: When initializing a project, Terraform should check the central directory and create a hard link or reference rather than copying the binary. This saves disk space while maintaining compatibility.

Checksum and Lockfile Integration: Ensure compatibility with .terraform.lock.hcl and provider checksum validation so that reproducibility and integrity remain intact.

Backwards Compatibility: Projects that don’t opt into this centralised mode should continue functioning normally using the current behaviour.

Configuration Example (Hypothetical):
# .terraformrc or terraform CLI config
```hcl
provider_cache {
  central_directory = "~/.terraform/providers"
  mode              = "shared"
}```

### Terraform Version

```shell
1.12.2
```

### Use Cases

When refactoring Terraform code, for example when introducing `foreach` blocks, one can sometimes generate plans which have create/delete pairs that exist only because the Terraform id has changed. 

For example, that might look like this:

```

  # aws_organizations_policy_attachment.allowlist will be destroyed
  # (because aws_organizations_policy_attachment.allowlist is not in configuration)
  - resource "aws_organizations_policy_attachment" "blah_foo" {
      - id        = "ou-iciu-foo:blah:p-foo" -> null
      - policy_id = "p-blah" -> null
      - target_id = "ou-iciu-foo" -> null
    }

  # aws_organizations_policy_attachment.allowlist["ou-iciu-foo"] will be created
  + resource "aws_organizations_policy_attachment" "service_allowlist_foo" {
      + id        = (known after apply)
      + policy_id = "p-blah"
      + target_id = "ou-iciu-foo"
    }
```

(This is a minimal example; the actual plan might of course be very large.)

### Attempted Solutions

There are some existing workarounds:
* Add a `moved` block, although you have to manually specify the right IDs, and I see there are some other bugs like https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/35785 about limitations there 
* Do imperative state surgery

### Proposal

I see there's quite a few issues about this general area but I think this suggestion is new – apologies if not.

It seems to me that Terraform, looking at the plan, can see that a resource is being deleted and an identical resource is being created and it could simplify this to be just a rename.

In this example, zero changes are needed at the AWS API level, Terraform just needs to record a new binding between the AWS ARN and the Terraform-side id. 

Think of this as similar to how git infers renames from create/delete of files. 

This would have some UX benefits:
* The plan would be smaller and easier to review for correctness
* For many cases, users would not need to learn about and correctly write `move` blocks, keeping their source smaller

Making fewer mutating operations has technical benefits too:
* In this case, the application failed because Terraform tried to create the new policy attachment before deleting the old one, which was rejected by AWS because it creates a duplicate
* Making fewer changes means the application passes through fewer intermediate states, which may cause unexpected and unwanted behavior: for example by having neither policy attached. These intermediate steps are undesirable even if brief but especially if the apply operation fails or is interrupted.
* The apply operation can simply be faster if it eliminates unnecessary blocking API calls

Implementing this approach may require adding a concept of resources being identical and reusable. I don't know enough about the Terraform internals for this. Resources that have internal state like VMs or databases wouldn't be applicable, but the great majority of resources in the tree I work on seem to be "value objects": if they have exactly the same attributes then it's the same object. An IAM policy attachment is a good example of where you never care about its unique identity, and probably that would also be true for the policies themselves.

Following the example of git one can imagine it also inferring "rename and then change" operations but that seems more complex and could be left for later. 

Thanks for considering it!

### References

_No response_
issues.title: Infer resource moves automatically?

module "example" {

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.13.4
on darwin_arm64
```

### Use Cases

When writing big numbers it is hard to visually see what number it is. For a concrete example, the `terraform-aws-provider` supports the `cloudwatch_metric_alarm` resource which has a field called `threshold` (see https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/aws/latest/docs/resources/cloudwatch_metric_alarm#threshold-1).

You can use this resource to create an alert in AWS Cloudwatch if a specific value does not pass the check. In case of storage, the value has to be written in bytes. Representing a GB will make your write a number such as `1000000000` which is really hard to read. You could work around it by doing 1000 * 1000 * 1000 instead.

The same is true for numbers that represent seconds in resources. Usually its better to do a calculation to make the user aware of that fact.

### Attempted Solutions

As mentioned above, instead of writing the number, it can be replaced with a calculation that represents the number e.g.
`1000000000 -> 1000 * 1000 * 1000`
`86400 -> 60 * 60 * 24`

### Proposal

Before I propose a solution, please be aware of the following:

Neither go nor JSON natively support a way to "pretty-print" numbers in code. Thus, it would be a custom feature to terraform/HCL to recognize such numbers.

Proposal:
Allow numbers to be written in a way that separates the value of thousand for better readability of the code. Which separator to be used is up to the implementation.

Suggestions are `,` (C#, Python), `'` or `_`.

### Terraform Version

### Use Cases

Just improving the speed of Terraform, updating it with new GoLang features that are faster and more semantic-sugar-like.

### Attempted Solutions

I'd open a PR to update the cases of the `rangeint` matches from modernize I found, but I don't want to spend time on it if it won't receive attention by the maintainers.

### Proposal

https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/tools/gopls/internal/analysis/modernize has a list of suggestions to update to use features in newer GoLang versions. Based on a quick search, the rangeint replacement suggestion seems to be slightly faster, and in any case, it looks more GoLang-ish.

```
rangeint: replace a 3-clause "for i := 0; i < n; i++" loop by "for i := range n", added in go1.22.

### Terraform Version

```shell
N/A
```

### Use Cases

I have a use-case where I need to occasionally taint a resource so that it gets recreated. To give a little bit of detail, we create some azure postgres flexible servers with HA enabled and configured terraform as an admin with the `azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_active_directory_administrator` resource so that terraform can login to the server with the `cyrilgdn/postgresql` provider using an entra token instead of a password. This works well until the DB server fails over to the standby server. The standby, for whatever reason, doesn't have the administrators defined, so we had to taint the resource in terraform state in order to have the resource created again on the standby.

### Attempted Solutions

I tried to setup something to detect when the zone changes and recreate the ad administrator resources, but it is a bit brittle, and if it's pushed to try to recreate the resources in question when no failover has occurred, then the delete API just hangs indefinitely (seemingly due to ownership of objects, but that is debatable), ultimately resulting in a terraform timeout. So the answer to this that seems most obvious to me to both avoid needing to run imperative commands, and avoid this timeout, is to simply put a boolean flag in the lifecycle block that simply tells terraform to recreate the resource.

Alternatively, I need to write `removed {}` blocks when a server fails over, then run terraform apply to remove those resources from state, then remove those `removed {}` blocks and run another terraform apply to recreate those resources.

### Proposal

It would be very useful to us if we have something like a boolean `lifecycle.tainted` meta argument that we can set to true or false in the code for the resource to let terraform know to mark the resource tainted and recreate it when we need to, without having to use the imperative `terraform taint` command.

### References

hashicorp/terraform-provider-azurerm#24736 details the failure to destroy the `azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server_active_directory_administrator` resources.

issues.body:
## Background

Terraform's codebase has separate concepts of state and state _files_. A state could be empty (no resources/data sources/outputs/checks etc) but a state file cannot be empty as it'll always contain data like the Terraform version, lineage etc. An empty state's state file is represented by a JSON object like this:

```json
{
  "version": 4,
  "terraform_version": "1.14.0",
  "serial": 4,
  "lineage": "a0f911d6-cc86-a0d6-4d4c-967c11b80966",
  "outputs": {},
  "resources": [],
  "check_results": null
}
```

Currently when state file data is written to a remote location (i.e. a remote-state backends like `s3`) Terraform constructs a state file, which may or may not include state data, and then passes the bytes of that state file to the `Put` method of the client used for interacting with that external service:

https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/053738fbf08d50261eccb463580525b88f461d8e/internal/states/remote/state.go#L205-L216

Due to how this code is written, the Put method is always guaranteed to receive a non-zero number of bytes. And this is correct; it is not valid for Terraform to attempt to write 0 bytes to a remote file.

In contrast, it is [valid for Terraform to receive 0 bytes when trying to read a remote state](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/053738fbf08d50261eccb463580525b88f461d8e/internal/states/remote/state.go#L143-L149), because that remote state file may not exist.

## Out of scope

This issue doesn't include state storage on the local filesystem.

This issue is relevant to the [remote-state backends](https://github.com/Vasist10/terraform/tree/main/internal/backend/remote-state) _but_ each backend has its own implementation of a remote client. Ideally the `Put` method of those backends' clients would defend against bad input, but that would need to be implemented repeatedly for each backend. We'd like to avoid sweeping changes that touch all backends 😅 .

## Proposal

There should be an explicit check to ensure that Terraform doesn't attempt to write 0 bytes to a pluggable state store, because that's always invalid.

This check could be implemented prior to [this line](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/e8631898c99cbc200e4088d7d748cfeb9799c161/internal/states/remote/state.go#L213) that calls a remote clients' `Put` method, or implemented in the `Put` methods of individual remote client implementations themselves.

In future any implementations of pluggable state storage will all go through a single path: [`grpcClient`'s implementation of `Put`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/d884031b4bfda113943efc2274f7539511adeed1/internal/states/remote/remote_grpc.go#L81), so this is a good location for a check that asserts the incoming slice of bytes is not empty.

There is an equivalent check in the filesystem state manager (i.e. implementation of `local` backend's state storage on the local filesystem) that responds to a nil state file input by creating an empty state file:

https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/d884031b4bfda113943efc2274f7539511adeed1/internal/states/statemgr/filesystem.go#L185-L188

I don't think this is a good approach when dealing with _remote_ states. Instead of responding to a complete lack of data by supplying bytes for an empty data set (which could overwrite something) Terraform should instead raise an error diagnostic to return to the user. That will alert the user something is wrong while avoiding any existing state being impacted by the bug.
issues.title: In the context of PSS, add explicit check to prevent Terraform attempting to write 0 bytes to a state file

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
1.x
```

### Use Cases

Currently, when Terraform initializes a provider, it spawns the provider plugin as a child process. By default, this child process inherits the entire environment context of the parent terraform CLI process.

This means that if I run terraform apply, every configured provider (AWS, Azure, Kubernetes, etc.) has visibility into every environment variable present in the shell (e.g., `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `ARM_CLIENT_ID`), regardless of whether that specific provider needs them.

---

The current behavior violates the principle of **Least Privilege** and leads to configuration conflicts in complex environments:

1. **Security/Leakage**: A compromised or malicious provider plugin (or a third-party community provider) theoretically has access to credentials meant for other providers (e.g., a Datadog provider process can read my AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY).
2. **Implicit Auth Conflicts**: When using multiple aliases for the same provider (e.g., aws.prod and aws.dev), accidentally set shell variables (like AWS_PROFILE) can override explicit HCL configurations if the provider precedence logic favors environment variables.
3. **CI/CD Hygiene**: In CI pipelines where many secrets are injected as env vars, it is difficult to isolate which secrets are visible to which step without complex shell wrappers.

### Attempted Solutions

For now the only way to do it is by using remote vault ephemeral data

### Proposal

I propose adding a meta-argument to the provider block (or a global setting) that allows users to explicitly whitelist which environment variables are passed to the plugin process.

If this list is present, the Terraform Core should filter the environment passed to the go-plugin client, sending only the matching keys.

----
### Proposed Syntax
**Option 1 (preferred): Allow-list per provider This would be non-breaking. If omitted, behavior defaults to "inherit all."**

```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
  
  # New Feature: Only pass these specific env vars to the plugin process
  # The plugin will not see GITHUB_TOKEN or other unrelated vars.
  allowed_environment_variables = ["AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY", "AWS_SESSION_TOKEN"]
}
```

**Option 2: Strict Isolation (Boolean) A flag to strictly disable all env var inheritance, forcing the user to rely solely on input variables defined in the HCL.**

```hcl
provider "google" {
  project = "my-project"
  
  # New Feature: The plugin process starts with an empty environment
  isolate_environment = true 
}
```



### References

_No response_

### Terraform Version

```shell
v1.14
```

### Use Cases

When dealing with difficult APIs for which a working provider does not exist it is sometimes pragmatically necessary to resort to using provisioners to invoke scripts to call those difficult APIs for external system configuration setup and (eventual) removal.  Obviously this is suboptimal, but unless you are able to code in _go_ and build a new provider or fix existing provider shortcomings for yourself, the only other option is to not use Terraform at all.

To be crystal clear up front, I acknowledge and understand that this is not the intended use of local-exec provisioners.

The feature I am requesting is a way to perform external non-terraform resource configuration _validation_ (during plan) and _update_ (during apply) via provisioners (typically on terraform_data resources).

### Attempted Solutions

N/A

### Proposal

I am in this unfortunate situation and currently have to use a terraform_data resource with a **when=create** local-exec provisioner to configure the target system and a **when=destroy** local-exec provisioner to later remove that configuration.  At a simplistic level this works, but (obviously) it has the downside of not allowing terraform to check/validate and update the configuration of the target system if necessary, each time it runs.

The feature I am requesting is a way to perform external _validation_ (during plan) and _update_ (during apply).  It might be done via two **when** values using the proposed example syntax below.  If a **validate** provisioner failed during plan, the resource would be flagged to indicate that any **update** provisioners need to be called during apply.

```
provisioner "local-exec" {
    when = validate
    command = "...."    # Check the external system and fail if it's not configured correctly
}

provisioner "local-exec" {
    when = update
    command = "...."     # Fix up the external system's incorrect configuration
```

There are some obvious variations to this approach that would likely be equally effective, like simply having a failing **validate** provisioner mark the resource as tainted so the **create** provisioners would then be called during apply.  This would mean the **create** provisioner would then be responsible for detecting any existing partially-completed configuration and fixing it, rather than starting from scratch (although well-written local-exec scripts would be doing this already).

Here's another possible syntax that would allow for more controlled validation/update of external configuration via provisioners:

```
provisioner "local-exec" {
    validate_command = "...."
    update_command = "...."
}
```

The intention here should be clear enough: call the validate_command during plan, and the update_command during apply if the validate_command fails.

I realise this is likely to be an unpopular request with the development team, since I'm asking them to add functionality purely to deal with other peoples' failure to build terraform provider components correctly.  I'm only asking because I am the poor bunny who is currently stuck between a rock and hard place :-(

### References

None found

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.15.0-dev
on darwin_arm64
```

### Use Cases

Users that habitually check the validity of their config using `terraform validate` should be able to detect when a `replace_triggered_by` attribute references an attribute that doesn't exist in that reference's schema. Updating the `validate` command would allow errors like this to be fixed before they cause disruption to a plan-apply workflow.

### Attempted Solutions

There isn't really a work around for this FR other than proceeding with plan-apply workflows and waiting for an error to occur, following the new error detection in the PR mentioned above.

### Proposal

This FR follows https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/36740. That issue, and the PR that closed it, allow users to detect this issue when creating a plan (either in plan or apply).  This means users would only realise that there is a defect in their configuration when that defect would impact a plan, not when it first enters the configuration. Also, the logic detecting bad `replace_triggered_by` references during plan would only be triggered if the resource referenced via `replace_triggered_by` is changed in a plan, so it's possible for a defect to be undetected until several plan-apply cycles have passed.

I propose that the `terraform validate` command should be updated to perform similar validation as in the PR that closed the issue above. This would allow users that habitually check the validity of their config to detect the defect early.

### References

- https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/36740
- https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/38010



Implementation wise, I believe this the code for validation would be in:

https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/c36c81431a0a6ee58e64b4fa70b82d8f0766ac56/internal/terraform/node_resource_validate.go#L283

The `validate` command constructs a graph and walks the 'validatable nodes' within that graph. That logic above is used when validating resources.

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.14.3
on darwin_arm64
```

### Use Cases

I want to discover existing cloud infrastructure using `terraform query` and import it into **existing** Terraform resource definitions.

**Scenario:** I have Terraform modules with protected resources:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "existing_data_lake" {
  bucket = "my-data-lake"

  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}
```

These resources often predate the current Terraform codebase, were created manually, or exist across multiple environments with different IDs.

**End goal:** Discover which cloud resources match my protected resource definitions, then import them into my existing handles - not create new resource blocks.

Currently, `-generate-config-out` assumes I want to create new resources. It generates auto-numbered addresses like `aws_s3_bucket.sample_0` and full resource blocks that conflict with my existing definitions.

There is no way to tell it "import into my existing `aws_s3_bucket.data_lake` handle."


### Attempted Solutions

I tried using grep/sed to parse the output of `terraform query -generate-config-out` and rewrite the `to` addresses to point to my existing resource handles.

The generated output looks like this:

```hcl
# __generated__ by Terraform
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "sample_0" { ... }

import {
  to = aws_s3_bucket.sample_0
  # ...
}
```

I need to change `to = aws_s3_bucket.sample_0` to `to = aws_s3_bucket.data_lake` (my existing handle), then discard the generated resource block.

A native mapping mechanism would be cleaner than external HCL parsing, which feels fragile.


### Proposal

Add a way to map query results to existing resource addresses.

**Option A - Companion block:**

```hcl
list "aws_s3_bucket" "buckets_query" {
  provider = aws
  config {}
}

import_target {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.buckets_query
  to   = aws_s3_bucket.existing_data_lake
}
```

**Option B - CLI mapping file:**

```bash
terraform query -generate-config-out=imports.tf -import-mapping=mapping.json
```

```json
{
  "aws_s3_bucket.buckets_query": "aws_s3_bucket.existing_data_lake"
}
```

**Expected behavior:**
- Output only `import {}` blocks (no resource blocks) when mapping is provided
- Error on cardinality mismatch (query returns N, target is singular)

---

Hope these ideas help, keen to see what approach others would take on this.

_No response_

issues.body: ### Terraform Version ```shell Terraform v1.9.2 ``` ### Use Cases When running terraform plan, resources that require replacement are currently represented as both an addition and a destruction in the final plan summary, for example: `Plan: 4 to add, 21 to change, 4 to destroy.` In real-world usage—especially in CI/CD pipelines, large infrastructures, and production environments—this summary can be confusing because: - A replacement is conceptually a single operation, not two independent actions - The final summary does not clearly communicate how many resources are being replaced - Users must manually scan the plan output (-/+) to understand what is actually happening - This increases cognitive load during reviews and approvals This becomes more problematic for: - Pull request reviews - Approval workflows based on plan summaries - New Terraform users - Large plans with mixed create/update/replace operations The goal is to improve clarity and usability of the terraform plan summary without changing Terraform behavior. ### Attempted Solutions Currently, replacements can only be identified by manually inspecting the detailed plan output for -/+ markers. Example: ``` -/+ resource "null_resource" "webapi_health_check" { ~ triggers = { ~ "always_run" = "2026-01-16T04:59:40Z" -> (known after apply) } } ``` Final summary: `Plan: 4 to add, 21 to change, 4 to destroy.` In this case, there may be no true new resources and no true deletions, only replacements, yet the summary suggests otherwise. There is no built-in way in Terraform Core to clearly summarize replacements at a high level. ### Proposal Enhance the `terraform plan` summary to explicitly report resource replacements. Example (Conceptual): ``` Plan Summary: 4 to replace 21 to change 0 to add 0 to destroy ``` Or a concise format: ``` Plan: 21 to change, 4 to replace. ``` Notes ``` This is a UX / presentation-only change No impact on state, apply logic, or execution order Terraform already internally identifies replacements (-/+) Improves readability, review confidence, and onboarding experience ``` Why This Helps - Reduces confusion between replacement and destruction - Improves plan review quality in CI/CD pipelines - Makes Terraform behavior easier to explain to non-experts - Enhances overall user experience with minimal behavioral change I understand this may seem like a small or unusual request, but it could significantly improve day-to-day usability for many Terraform users. ### References _No response_
issues.title: [Feature] Improve terraform plan output by summarizing replacements separately from add/destroy counts

The contents of the plan are collapsed - so users can chose to see it, but a summary is displayed: I think adding moved to the plan summary would be helpful on CLI and in tooling like pictured above. ### Attempted Solutions I wrote some stuff that would parse the plan output and tell me things moved - but it was wonky and complicated. It would be so much cleaner if terraform itself provided the info in the summary. ### Proposal Add a move count to the `ChangeSummary` struct and include it in the plan summary output. A resource is considered "moved" when its current address differs from its previous address (i.e., it was relocated via a `move{}` block). This count is independent of other actions - a resource can be moved _and_ updated/created/destroyed, and would appear in both counts. Example output: ``` Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy, 1 to move. ``` The move count would only be displayed when greater than zero to keep the common case clean. This applies to both human-readable output and JSON output (adding a "move" field to the change summary JSON). ### References _No response_

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.14.3
```

### Use Cases

In some workflows, it is desirable for a variable value to reference a resource or module output indirectly, without hard-coding that reference at the call site.

A common example is when variables are used as configuration inputs for actions, data sources, or downstream modules, and the source of the value may vary across environments or implementations.

Example use case:

- A reusable module or action expects a variable representing a resource-derived value (e.g., a Lambda function name).
- The calling configuration wants to supply that value by reference, not as a literal string.
- Today, variables only support literal defaults or expressions resolvable at variable definition time, not references to resources or modules defined elsewhere in the configuration.

This forces one of the following patterns:

- Threading resource outputs explicitly through every call site
- Duplicating references at usage points
- Avoiding variables altogether and coupling consumers directly to resource names

### Attempted Solutions

I attempted to express a resource output reference as a variable default, for example:

```

variable "aws_lambda_function_name_output_path" {
  description = "Path to the lambda function name output"
  type        = string
  default     = "${aws_lambda_function.example.function_name}"
}
```


However, Terraform treats this as invalid because variables cannot reference resources or module outputs.

I also experimented with escaping the expression so it could be interpreted later, for example:

`default = "$${aws_lambda_function.example.function_name}"`


But this is currently treated as a literal string, with no mechanism for deferred interpolation.

### Proposal

Introduce a supported mechanism for deferred or expression-based variable evaluation, allowing variables to reference resource or module outputs after graph construction, without violating Terraform’s dependency model.

One possible design (illustrative, not prescriptive):

```
variable "aws_lambda_function_name_output_path" {
  type    = string
  default = expr(aws_lambda_function.example.function_name)
}

```

or an explicit opt-in syntax for deferred interpolation:

`default = "$${aws_lambda_function.example.function_name}"`


Under this model:

- The variable value is not resolved during variable loading.
- The value is evaluated during graph execution, similar to how resource arguments are resolved.
- Terraform can still infer dependencies based on the referenced resource or module.

This would allow configurations such as:

```
resource "aws_lambda_function" "example" {
  # ...
}

action "aws_lambda_invoke" "example" {
  config {
    function_name = var.aws_lambda_function_name_output_path
    payload = jsonencode({
      key1 = "value1"
      key2 = "value2"
    })
  }
}
```

without forcing consumers to inline the resource reference directly.

**Why This Is Useful**

- Enables more reusable and decoupled modules
- Reduces repetitive wiring of outputs through multiple layers
- Allows configuration-driven indirection without resorting to locals or hard-coded references
- Preserves Terraform’s dependency graph while improving expressiveness

This feature would be especially useful for:

- Actions and providers that accept resource-derived identifiers
- Meta-modules that orchestrate resources without tightly coupling to them
- Advanced automation workflows where values are selected by configuration rather than structure

### References

_No response_
issues.title: Support Deferred / Expression-Based Evaluation of Variables Referencing Resource or Module Outputs

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.14.3
```

### Use Cases

Terraform variables are values, not expressions. If a user passes a string that looks like an expression (e.g., ${upper("test")}), Terraform treats it as a literal string (or it is rejected depending on context). There is currently no supported mechanism to:

1. Pass an expression via a variable (including Terraform functions), and
3. Have Terraform evaluate that expression when the variable is used as an argument to a resource or module.

This prevents certain “configuration-driven indirection” patterns, such as:

- Passing a naming rule or formatting rule as configuration
- Having a module accept a “value expression” to compute a final name/path/ID
- Avoiding repeated boilerplate expressions across multiple call sites/resources
- Driving transformations from environment configuration without duplicating expression logic


```
variable "function_name_rule" {
  type = string
}

# Caller wants:
# function_name_rule = "$${upper(var.base_name)}"

resource "aws_lambda_function" "example" {
  function_name = var.function_name_rule   # would be ideal if evaluated here
}

```

### Attempted Solutions

Using interpolation-like syntax inside a string, such as:

`function_name_rule = "$${upper("test")}"`

Terraform currently treats this as a literal string; there is no supported evaluation step to interpret it as an expression.

- Workarounds like locals or duplicating the expression at each use site defeat the goal of configuration-driven reuse.

### Proposal

Introduce an opt-in, explicit way to represent deferred expressions as a distinct type/value that can be passed through variables and evaluated at the point of use in resource/module arguments.

### **Option A: New Expression Value Constructor + Explicit Evaluation**

**Call site:**
```

variable "name_expr" {
  type = expr(string) # or a dedicated expression type
}

module "x" {
  source    = "./x"
  name_expr = expr(upper("test"))
}

```

**Inside module or resource usage:**

```
resource "aws_lambda_function" "example" {
  function_name = eval(var.name_expr)
}

```

Properties:

- expr(...) produces an expression value (not a string)
- eval(...) explicitly evaluates it in the current scope at the point of use
- Terraform can validate types (expr(string)), and prevent arbitrary evaluation where not permitted
- Keeps evaluation explicit (no “magic string interpolation”)

Option B: String-Based Deferred Interpolation

Allow a string convention like $${ ... } anywhere variables are used, and evaluate it at use sites. Example:

`function_name = "$${upper("test")}"`

This is more ergonomic, but is also more ambiguous, harder to statically analyze, and risks confusing “data” vs “code”.

Why This Is Useful

- Enables reusable “rules” for naming/formatting without repeating expressions
- Allows modules to accept transformation logic from callers in a controlled way
- Improves ergonomics for environments with strong naming conventions
- Keeps dependency graph correctness if expression evaluation still flows through Terraform’s standard expression model

### References

_No response_
issues.title: Support Passing and Evaluating Deferred Expressions (Functions) via Variables at Point of Use

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.11.4
on linux_amd64
```

### Use Cases

I'm using Terraform to stage VM templates (disk images and configuration) for later replication to multiple VM hosts, for the disk images, I'm creating symlinks and using `rsync -L` to avoid unnecessary copies.

I'm currently creating the symlinks with resources like the following:

```
resource "terraform_data" "disk_symlink" {
  triggers_replace = [
    abspath(local.image_path),
    "${ var.template_dir }/${ local.output_image_name }",
  ]

  input = [
    abspath(local.image_path),
    "${ var.template_dir }/${ local.output_image_name }",
  ]

  provisioner "local-exec" {
    environment = {
      SOURCE = self.output[0]
      DEST = self.output[1]
    }

    command = "mkdir -p \"$(dirname \"$DEST\")\" && ln -s \"$SOURCE\" \"$DEST\""
  }

  provisioner "local-exec" {
    when       = destroy
    on_failure = continue

    environment = {
      DEST = self.output[1]
    }

    command = "rm -f \"$DEST\""
  }
}
```

This works and updates the symlink when either the source or destination is changed, but it doesn't gracefully handle either the link pre-existing, or being deleted by something outside of Terraform.

### Attempted Solutions

See above.

### Proposal

It would be nice if there was a `local_symlink` resource which integrated what the above example does and also correctly fixes the state when something else creates/deletes/changes the link.

```
resource "local_symlink" "foo" {
  target = "foo"
  filename = "${path.module}/foo.bar"
}
```

### Terraform Version ```shell Terraform v1.14.3 on linux_amd64 ``` ### Use Cases When running `terraform plan` on large infrastructure stacks, the output can span thousands of lines. Engineers must scroll extensively to understand the scope of changes. While the final line summarizes the counts (`Plan: X to add, Y to change, Z to destroy`), it lacks context on which resources are affected without scrolling back up, potentially losing the buffer history. Furthermore, "Replacements" are technically counted as add/destroy pairs in the stats but are logically a single action for the operator. The current "wall of text" makes it prone to human error (missing a critical destroy action hidden among updates). ### Attempted Solutions I developed a wrapper script to demonstrate the utility of this view. It converts the plan to JSON and groups outputs. Logic demonstrated: - Groups by Action (Add, Change, Destroy). - Explicitly detects Replacements (resources with both create and delete actions in the changeset) and separates them from pure adds/destroys. - Lists only the resource addresses. This is a very raw script and provided only as Proof of Concept
Details

```sh #!/bin/bash #################################################### # ARGS # Check invocation mode quiet=false if [[ "$1" == "quiet" ]]; then quiet=true shift # Remove the "quiet" argument fi debug=false if [[ "$1" == "debug" ]]; then debug=true shift # Remove the "debug" argument fi #################################################### # FUNCTIONS # Produce an echo message when quiet mode is FALSE log() { if ! $quiet then echo "$@" # Print all arguments passed to the function fi } # Produce an echo message when quiet mode is log_on_quiet() { if $quiet then echo "$@" # Print all arguments passed to the function fi } # Define if a string is a json is_json() { if jq -e . <<< "$1" > /dev/null 2>&1; then return 0 # True else return 1 # False fi } # Text functions green_bold() { printf "\e[1;32m%s\e[0m" "$1"; } orange_bold() { printf "\e[1;38;5;208m%s\e[0m" "$1"; } red_bold() { printf "\e[1;31m%s\e[0m" "$1"; } blue_bold() { printf "\e[1;34m%s\e[0m" "$1"; } cyan_bold() { printf "\e[1;36m%s\e[0m" "$1"; } light_red() { printf "\e[38;5;9m%s\e[0m" "$1"; } light_green() { printf "\e[38;5;10m%s\e[0m" "$1"; } italic() { printf "\e[3m%s\e[0m" "$1"; } #################################################### # EXECUTION # Define a temporary file for the plan output TMP_PLAN="$(tempfile)" TMP_JSON="$TMP_PLAN.json" # Create plan if $quiet; then terraform plan -out="$TMP_PLAN" &> /dev/null else terraform plan -out="$TMP_PLAN" fi # Check if the plan command completed with success if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then echo "terraform plan failed" exit 1 fi log "Creating summary..." # Converting the plan to json terraform show -no-color -json "$TMP_PLAN" > "$TMP_JSON" # Extracting numbers COUNT_CREATE=$(jq '.resource_changes | map(select(.change.actions | length == 1 and .[0] == "create")) | length' "$TMP_JSON") COUNT_UPDATE=$(jq '.resource_changes | map(select(.change.actions | length == 1 and .[0] == "update")) | length' "$TMP_JSON") COUNT_DELETE=$(jq '.resource_changes | map(select(.change.actions | length == 1 and .[0] == "delete")) | length' "$TMP_JSON") COUNT_REPLACE=$(jq -r '.resource_changes | map(select(.change.actions | type == "array" and length == 2 and all(["create", "delete"] | map(IN(.))))) | length' "$TMP_JSON") #################################################### # OUTPUT # Create numerics message plan_message="Plan: " if [[ "$COUNT_CREATE" -gt 0 ]]; then plan_message+="$(green_bold "$COUNT_CREATE to add")" else plan_message+="$COUNT_CREATE to add" fi plan_message+="," if [[ "$COUNT_UPDATE" -gt 0 ]]; then plan_message+=" $(orange_bold "$COUNT_UPDATE to change")" else plan_message+=" $COUNT_UPDATE to change" fi plan_message+="," if [[ "$COUNT_DELETE" -gt 0 ]]; then plan_message+=" $(red_bold "$COUNT_DELETE to destroy")" else plan_message+=" $COUNT_DELETE to destroy" fi plan_message+="," if [[ "$COUNT_REPLACE" -gt 0 ]]; then plan_message+=" $(blue_bold "$COUNT_REPLACE to replace")" else plan_message+=" $COUNT_REPLACE to replace" fi echo "$plan_message." echo "" # No actions found, found no differences if [[ "$COUNT_CREATE" -eq 0 && "$COUNT_UPDATE" -eq 0 && "$COUNT_DELETE" -eq 0 && "$COUNT_REPLACE" -eq 0 ]] then # If quiet=FALSE there is already the entire plan log available, no need to replicate the summary log_on_quiet "$(green_bold "No changes"). Your infrastructure matches the configuration." log_on_quiet "Terraform has compared your real infrastructure against your configuration and found no differences, so no changes are needed." exit 0 fi # Printing summary # ---------------- CREATE ---------------- if [[ "$COUNT_CREATE" -gt 0 ]] then echo "---------- $(green_bold "ADD ($COUNT_CREATE)") ----------" jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | length == 1 and .[0] == "create") | "- " + .address' "$TMP_JSON" echo "" fi # ---------------- UPDATE ---------------- if [[ "$COUNT_UPDATE" -gt 0 ]] then echo "---------- $(orange_bold "CHANGE ($COUNT_UPDATE)") ----------" jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | length == 1 and .[0] == "update") | "- " + .address' "$TMP_JSON" echo "" fi # ---------------- DELETE ---------------- if [[ "$COUNT_DELETE" -gt 0 ]] then echo "---------- $(red_bold "DESTROY ($COUNT_DELETE)") ----------" jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | length == 1 and .[0] == "delete") | "- " + .address' "$TMP_JSON" echo "" fi # ---------------- REPLACE ---------------- if [[ "$COUNT_REPLACE" -gt 0 ]] then echo "---------- $(blue_bold "REPLACE ($COUNT_REPLACE)") ----------" # Simple list, not used anymore # jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | length == 2 and contains(["create", "delete"])) | .address' "$TMP_JSON" # Replaces are decorated with additional details, process each item individually addresses=($(jq -r '.resource_changes[] | select(.change.actions | length == 2 and contains(["create", "delete"])) | .address' "$TMP_JSON")) for address in "${addresses[@]}"; do echo "- $address" # Retrieve the json definition of the single replace item (address may contain " as part of a module reference) item=$(jq -r --arg addr "$address" '.resource_changes[] | select(.address == $addr)' "$TMP_JSON") # Retrieve the reason for the replace reason=$(echo "$item" | jq -r '.action_reason') echo " reason: $reason" # replace_paths example#1: "replace_paths": [ ["name"] ] # Check if objects contains "replace_paths" so that we can provide more insight of what is chaning if jq -e '.change.replace_paths' <<< "$item" > /dev/null 2>&1; then # If replace_paths exists, I select only the items with 1 element, and from them I select the first element jq -c '.change.replace_paths[] | .[0]' <<< "$item" | while read single_element; do #echo "test: $single_element" before_value=$(echo "$item" | jq -r ".change.before.$single_element") after_value=$(echo "$item" | jq -r ".change.after.$single_element") echo " $single_element: $(italic "$(light_red "$before_value")") => $(italic "$(light_green "$after_value")")" done fi done echo "" fi #################################################### # CLEAN UP # Remove temporary files if ! $debug; then rm "$TMP_PLAN" rm "$TMP_JSON" else echo "Debug Mode: temporary files are preserved" echo "$TMP_PLAN" echo "$TMP_JSON" fi ```

This is an example of the resulting output: ### Proposal I propose a native flag, e.g., `terraform plan -summary`, or a config option that prints a concise table/list at the very end of the execution, grouping resources by action. While tools like `tf-summarize` or jq parsing exist, having a native, dependency-free way to verify the "high-level impact" of a plan directly in the binary is crucial for DevSecOps workflows and local debugging where installing external binaries might not be feasible or desired. ### References * https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/26261 * https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/33049
issues.title: Native CLI Summary View for Plan (-summary flag)

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
1.14.5
```

### Use Cases

Organizations that already run Elasticsearch as core infrastructure need a way to store Terraform remote state without introducing additional services. Currently, teams in this situation are forced to stand up a separate storage system (e.g. S3, Consul, Postgres) solely for Terraform state, adding operational overhead, additional credentials to manage, and another point of failure.

### Attempted Solutions

The closest existing option is the http backend, which could theoretically work by placing an HTTP proxy in front of Elasticsearch. However, this approach requires:
1. Writing and maintaining a separate intermediary service that translates between the HTTP backend protocol and Elasticsearch's API
2. Deploying and operating that service as additional infrastructure
3. Implementing state locking manually in the proxy layer, since the HTTP backend's locking support is limited

This defeats the purpose of using existing infrastructure -- it just trades one dependency (a state backend) for another (a custom proxy).

Example of what this workaround looks like:

```hcl
# Requires a custom proxy service running at this address
terraform {
  backend "http" {
    address        = "http://es-state-proxy:8080/state/myproject"
    lock_address   = "http://es-state-proxy:8080/lock/myproject"
    unlock_address = "http://es-state-proxy:8080/unlock/myproject"
  }
}
```

The consul and pg backends serve as precedent for supporting infrastructure that teams already operate. Elasticsearch falls into the same category.

### Proposal

A native elasticsearch backend that stores state as documents in an Elasticsearch index. Configuration would look like:

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "elasticsearch" {
    endpoints = ["https://elasticsearch.internal:9200"]
    index     = "terraform_remote_state"
    username  = "terraform"
    password  = "secret"
  }
}
```

Key design points of the implementation:
- Authentication: Supports username/password, API key, and bearer token (mutually exclusive, validated at configure time)
- TLS: Supports custom CA certificates, client certificates for mutual TLS, and skip-verification -- all via file paths or inline PEM, plus environment variable overrides
- Locking: Uses Elasticsearch's op_type=create for atomic lock acquisition -- no external lock service needed
- Workspaces: Each workspace gets its own state and lock document within the same index, identified by state-{workspace} and lock-{workspace} document IDs
- Index management: The backend auto-creates the index with appropriate mappings on first use
- Environment variables: All configuration fields can be set via ELASTICSEARCH_* environment variables
 
I have a working implementation with full test coverage and am willing to maintain this backend long-term. I'd like to add myself to CODEOWNERS for this backend.

The CONTRIBUTING.md notes that the team is not currently merging new state storage backends. I'm opening this issue to discuss whether an exception is possible given the willingness to maintain it long-term.

Existing community-maintained backends (pg, cos) serve as precedent for third-party-maintained backends in the repository.

### References

_No response_

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.14.5
on windows_amd64
```

### Use Cases

Sensitive values have many restrictions on their use, as they should. This makes sensitivity-propagation impactful for debugging why a value can't be used in a `for_each` block, or included in an output, or is being marked as `sensitive` in a plan, inter alia.

In the terraform console the following tests return expected values:

```
> { } == null
false
> null == null
true
> issensitive(null)
false
> issensitive({})
false
> issensitive({ } == null)
false
> issensitive({ foo = sensitive("secret") })
false
> issensitive({ foo = sensitive("secret") }.foo)
true
> issensitive({ foo = "not a secret" }.foo)
false
> issensitive({ foo = "not a secret" } == null)
false
> issensitive({ foo = sensitive("secret") } == { foo = "not a secret" } )
true
> issensitive(length([sensitive("secret")]))
false
> issensitive(length(sensitive(["secret"])))
true
```

But comparing a non-sensitive object with a sensitive sub-property to `null` produces an unexpected result:

```
> issensitive({ foo = sensitive("secret") } == null)
true
```

The value of the `sensitive` property has no impact on whether the parent object is `null` or not; therefore, it is unexpected that the result of the comparison operator should be marked as `sensitive`.

This is particularly pernicious when writing complicated expressions that don't involve the `sensitive` value at all; even other `nonsensitive`  properties end up getting marked as `sensitive` after the comparison:

```
> issensitive([ for a in [{ foo = sensitive("secret"), bar = "not a secret" }] : a.bar if a != null ][0])
true
```

### Attempted Solutions

This can be worked around by wrapping the `null` check in a `nonsensitive` block, like so:

```
> issensitive(nonsensitive({ foo = sensitive("secret") } == null))
false
```

Or by using `length` checks and arrays of `length` zero or one for `optional` values rather than objects that can be `null`.

The problem is not being able to solve the problem after it's been discovered; the problem is discovering that this is the root of the problem in the first place, especially in the face of complicated list-comprehensions.

### Proposal

Comparing an object with `sensitive` properties for equality to another non-`null` object must continue to result in a `sensitive` value. Comparing an object with `sensitive` properties for equality to another value which may or may not be `null` likely must continue to result in a `sensitive` value.

However, I would expect that comparisons between a `nonsensitive` object and a constant value known at parse time to be `nonsensitive` and `null` _should not_ result in a `sensitive` value.

That is:

```
> issensitive({ foo = sensitive("secret") } == null)
false
> issensitive({ foo = sensitive("secret") } != null)
false
```

Comparing objects to hard-coded `null` values is a common patten when dealing with `optional` sub-objects.

If this logic for the `sensitive` could be extended to the "value known only after `apply`" flag as well, this would also make terraform much more ergonomic when working with optional values derived from resource state that _can_ be known not to be `null` even before `apply`, even if we can't know _what particular value_ the property will be. Perhaps a "known to always be `null`" type-annotation could help in both cases.

### References

- #34061 This issue shows a developer being confused by direct comparison of `null` to a sensitive value; it is correct for the value to be `sensitive` in this case. I am not proposing to change this logic.
- #32868 This issue shows the sort of workarounds people propose when an entire object become marked `sensitive` unexpectedly; it becomes less important if `sensitive` values are propagated in more expected ways.
- #36370 shows another developer being confused by this issue, and why the `length` operator doesn't propagate `sensitive`s while the `!= null` does.
issues.title: Do Not Propagate `sensitive` Flag on Properties when Comparing a `nonsensitive` Object to `null`

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
1.14.6
```

### Use Cases

Terraform currently requires `count` or `for_each` to conditionally create resources or modules. Both approaches introduce indexing into the resource address (e.g., resource.name[0]), even when managing a single optional instance.

This behavior complicates configuration design, increases cognitive load, and makes refactoring more error-prone.

This request proposes introducing a native mechanism (e.g., enabled meta-argument) to conditionally create resources without changing their state address.

### Attempted Solutions

Today, conditional resource creation is typically implemented as:
```
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
  count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0
}
```

This results in:

`aws_s3_bucket.example[0]`

instead of:

`aws_s3_bucket.example`

### Key limitations:

1. **State address instability**
   - Introducing conditional logic requires changing resource addresses
   - Leads to state migrations or resource recreation risks

2. **Cascading complexity**
   - All dependent resources must reference indexed instances:
     ```hcl
     aws_s3_bucket.example[0].id
     ```
   - Requires conditional guards across the codebase

3. **Refactoring overhead**
   - Converting an existing resource into a conditional one forces address changes
   - Requires `terraform state mv` or manual intervention

4. **Mental overhead**
   - Engineers must always reason about indices, even for single-instance resources



### Proposal

Introduce a meta-argument (name TBD), for example:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
  enabled = var.enabled
}
```

or:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
  condition = var.enabled
}
```

### Expected behavior:

- `enabled = true` → resource is created as:
  ```
  aws_s3_bucket.example
  ```
- `enabled = false` → resource is not created
- No index (`[0]`) is introduced
- Resource address remains stable across lifecycle changes

---

## Design Considerations

### 1. State model

- Resource address should remain constant
- When disabled, resource is absent from state
- Re-enabling recreates the resource at the same address

---

### 2. Dependency handling

Terraform could:

- treat disabled resources as non-existent nodes in the graph
- surface clear errors if referenced while disabled

---

### 3. Backward compatibility

- No breaking changes required
- `count` / `for_each` remain fully supported
- New meta-argument is additive

---

### 4. Module support

The same mechanism should apply to modules:

```hcl
module "example" {
  source  = "./module"
  enabled = var.enabled
}
```

---

## Alternatives Considered

### `count`

- Introduces indexing
- Breaks address stability
- Adds complexity for single-instance use cases

### `for_each`

- Better semantics for collections
- Still introduces keyed addressing
- Overkill for simple boolean conditions

---

## Benefits

- Stable resource addressing
- Simplified configuration
- Easier refactoring of existing infrastructure
- Reduced cognitive overhead
- Cleaner module interfaces
- Improved readability and maintainability

---

## Additional Context

This limitation becomes more apparent in:

- large modular infrastructures
- long-lived Terraform states
- environments with frequent feature toggling
- identity and access management scenarios


### References

_No response_
issues.title: Conditional resource/module creation without index (count/for_each alternative)

### Use Cases

This would match the emerging consensus in the industry that upgrading to very recent releases poses an increasing risk of supply-chain attacks. Having a cooldown / minimum age period would give the community time to detect such attacks. Terraform is a tempting target since it is typically run with high-privilege credentials.

### Attempted Solutions

n/a

### Proposal

Add an option (via the usual CLI / config file / environmental variables) to set a minimum age to consider when evaluating module versions (e.g. “Do not install anything released in the last 7 days”). When running `terraform init --upgrade` the solver can ignore versions which were published after the cutoff date.

To allow high-priority updates or safe sources, it would be useful to implement an exclude mechanism either by disabling this feature for a single provider or module such as a trusted internal publisher or to define the logic such that it only applies when attempting to upgrade the pinned versions but never prevents a newer version when explicitly pinned in the provider / module version (e.g. `version = "1.2.3"` does not have the check applied but `version = "~> 1.2"` would treat yesterday's 1.2.3 as if it was never published and use last week's 1.2.2).

issues.body: ## Description When using the S3 backend with a non-AWS S3-compatible object storage (e.g., IBM Cleversafe/COS), `PutObject` requests fail with `403 AccessDenied` even though `skip_s3_checksum = true` is set in the backend configuration. The root cause is that `skip_s3_checksum` does not disable the AWS SDK v2's chunked transfer encoding and checksum trailer on `PutObject` requests. The SDK still sends: ``` content-encoding: aws-chunked x-amz-content-sha256: STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER x-amz-trailer: x-amz-checksum-crc32 ``` Many S3-compatible backends (IBM Cleversafe/COS, older MinIO, some Ceph RGW versions) do not support these headers and reject the request with `403 AccessDenied`. ## Terraform and Provider Version - Terraform: 1.14.8 - AWS SDK Go v2: 1.39.2 (bundled) - Backend: S3-compatible (IBM Cleversafe (dsNet) 3.18.5.48) ## Backend Configuration ```hcl terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = "my-bucket" key = "path/to/terraform.tfstate" endpoints = { s3 = "https://s3.example.com" } region = "us-east-1" skip_credentials_validation = true skip_metadata_api_check = true skip_region_validation = true skip_requesting_account_id = true use_path_style = true skip_s3_checksum = true encrypt = false } } ``` ## Observed Behavior `GET`, `HEAD`, and `ListObjectsV2` succeed. `PutObject` (state push/write) fails with 403. TRACE log shows the PutObject request includes chunked encoding headers despite `skip_s3_checksum = true`: ``` HTTP Request Sent: rpc.method=PutObject http.request.header.content_encoding=aws-chunked http.request.header.x_amz_content_sha256=STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER http.request.header.x_amz_trailer=x-amz-checksum-crc32 http.request.header.x_amz_decoded_content_length=64040 HTTP Response Received: rpc.method=PutObject http.status_code=403 AccessDeniedAccess Denied ``` ## Workaround Setting the AWS SDK v2 environment variable before running Terraform resolves the issue: ```bash export AWS_REQUEST_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION=WHEN_REQUIRED ``` This disables the automatic chunked checksum on PutObject. With this env var, `terraform state push` and all write operations succeed. ## Expected Behavior `skip_s3_checksum = true` should also disable the request-side `aws-chunked` content-encoding and checksum trailer on `PutObject`, not just response-side checksum validation. Alternatively: 1. Add a dedicated backend option (e.g., `skip_s3_chunked_encoding`) to control this behavior. 2. Document that `AWS_REQUEST_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION=WHEN_REQUIRED` is needed for S3-compatible backends that don't support chunked checksums. 3. Automatically set this SDK behavior when `skip_s3_checksum = true` is configured. ## Impact This affects any S3-compatible backend that does not support AWS SDK v2's chunked transfer encoding, including: - IBM Cloud Object Storage / Cleversafe - Older MinIO versions - Some Ceph RGW configurations Users relying on `skip_s3_checksum` for compatibility with non-AWS backends are still hitting write failures with no clear indication of the cause the 403 error is misleading and suggests a credentials/policy issue.
issues.title: S3 backend: skip_s3_checksum does not disable aws-chunked content-encoding on PutObject

##### Core requirements

- I want be able to get the associated endpoints for the existing ARC cluster within Terraform so that I can pass it through to other automation components as parameters.

##### Additional nice to haves

- Ability to query all clusters/control panels/routing controls/safety rules in an account.
- Ability to query details about a specific control panel/routing control/safety rule in an account.
- This may be deemed to not be a fit for the Terraform provider, if so, happy to ignore. Given a list of Route53 Recovery Controller ARC endpoints, I'd like to have an action that follows the AWS recommended consumption model for trying each endpoint one by one until one succeeds, attempting to change the state of a routing control.

### Use Cases

Allow `terraform validate` command to succeed without required validation of backend like s3 in AWS.
Especially useful in CI/CD where the backend is often supplied in the pipeline, rather than hardcoded in .tf files.

Currently we keep backend block empty:

```tf
  backend "s3" {
    # We build it inside CI/CD
  }
```

And in CICD run:

```yaml
          terraform init \
            -backend-config="region=${{ inputs.aws_default_region }}" \
            -backend-config="bucket=${BUCKET_NAME}" \
            -backend-config="key=${KEY_NAME}" \
            -backend-config="use_lockfile=true" \
            -backend-config="encrypt=true"

          terraform validate
```

Which currently fails in `v.1.15.0` with:
```
The argument "bucket" is required, but no definition was found.
The argument "key" is required, but no definition was found.
```

### Attempted Solutions

I tried:

1) ❌ 
```bash
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
```

2) ❌ 
```bash
tfdata="$(mktemp -d)"
TF_DATA_DIR="$tfdata" terraform init -backend=false
TF_DATA_DIR="$tfdata" terraform validate
```

3) ✅ 

```tf
  backend "s3" {
    # We build it inside CI/CD
    bucket = "something"
    key    = "something"
    region = "something"
  }
}
```

```bash
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
```

This succeeded but requires me to touch all our microservice repositories to change empty backend to fake backend.
Highly boring task.

### Proposal

Allow a flag for `terraform validate` command like:

```bash
terraform validate -no-backend
```

To skip this particular validation as it is supplied in GitHub Actions or other CI/CD tool.

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
1.15.1
```

### Use Cases

Terraform modules and root configurations are not inherently coupled to a particular state backend implementation, but Terraform currently forces this coupling by the backend type needing to be declared in the root configuration (minimum is the type).

### Attempted Solutions

The current workaround is to keep a minimal backend block in source, or generate one before terraform init, but both approaches still force execution-owned backend selection to appear as Terraform configuration.

### Proposal

Terraform currently supports partial backend configuration via `terraform init -backend-config=...`, but still requires the backend type itself to be declared in the root module configuration:

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {}
}
```

This creates a lifecycle mismatch.

A Terraform configuration describes an infrastructure graph. That graph is not inherently tied to a specific state backend implementation. The same root module can be equally valid when executed with `azurerm`, `s3`, `gcs`, `remote`, or another backend, depending on the automation platform, organization standards, deployment environment, or wrapper executing it.

For example, a reusable root configuration might be consumed by:

- an Azure DevOps pipeline using the `azurerm` backend
- a GitHub Actions workflow using the `s3` backend
- HCP Terraform using the `remote` / cloud workflow
- a local development workflow using the `local` backend

Those are execution concerns. They do not change the infrastructure model.

Terraform already acknowledges that backend configuration is partly execution-time context through `-backend-config`. However, only the backend attributes can be supplied this way. The backend type still has to be present in configuration source.

That split is difficult to justify conceptually:

```text
Execution context can provide:
- storage account
- bucket
- container
- key
- workspace
- tenant
- subscription
- credentials

Execution context cannot provide:
- backend type
```

In practice, backend type is part of the same execution lifecycle as the backend coordinates and credentials.

The current model means a Terraform configuration must declare an execution adapter even when the configuration itself does not care which backend implementation is used. Coupling these two things is unnecessary, and it makes reusable configurations less cleanly portable across execution environments.

Allow backend type to be selected explicitly during `terraform init`, for example:

```bash
terraform init \
  -backend=azurerm \
  -backend-config="tenant_id=..." \
  -backend-config="subscription_id=..." \
  -backend-config="resource_group_name=..." \
  -backend-config="storage_account_name=..." \
  -backend-config="container_name=tfstate" \
  -backend-config="key=solutionX-dev"
```

or:

```bash
terraform init \
  -backend=s3 \
  -backend-config="bucket=..." \
  -backend-config="region=..." \
  -backend-config="key=solutionX-dev"
```

When no backend block exists in configuration, Terraform would use the backend type supplied by `-backend`.

If both a backend block and `-backend` are present:

- if they match, proceed
- if they differ, fail loudly with a clear diagnostic

This would let automation fully own backend initialization:

```yaml
- script: |
    terraform init \
      -backend=azurerm \
      -backend-config="tenant_id=$(tenant_id)" \
      -backend-config="subscription_id=$(subscription_id)" \
      -backend-config="resource_group_name=$(resource_group_name)" \
      -backend-config="storage_account_name=$(storage_account_name)" \
      -backend-config="container_name=$(container_name)" \
      -backend-config="key=$(terraform_state_key)"
```

The Terraform source would then contain only the infrastructure model, while the execution environment owns state backend selection.

This can be introduced compatibly.

Existing backend blocks would continue to work:

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {}
}
```

Existing partial backend configuration would continue to work:

```bash
terraform init \
  -backend-config="key=solutionX-dev"
```

The new behavior would only apply when a user explicitly supplies a backend type, such as:

```bash
terraform init -backend=azurerm
```

This would also preserve a clear failure mode. If a root module declares:

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {}
}
```

and the caller runs:

```bash
terraform init -backend=azurerm
```

Terraform should fail before initialization with a diagnostic explaining that the configured backend type and supplied backend type differ.

This avoids silent backend changes while allowing execution-owned workflows to avoid committing a backend block.

---

### Design Considerations

A few likely objections are worth calling out explicitly.

#### Should `terraform validate` know about the backend?

It can, when the backend is declared fully in configuration source.

This proposal is not arguing that backend blocks are invalid or that Terraform should never validate them. For workflows that choose to declare a complete backend block in source, validating that block may be useful.

The concern is narrower: Terraform should not require backend information to be knowable from source in workflows that intentionally provide backend configuration at initialization time.

This was demonstrated by Terraform `1.15.0`, where validating backend block attributes broke workflows using partial backend configuration with `-backend-config`. Terraform `1.15.1` fixed that by removing backend attribute validation from `terraform validate`.

The same boundary can apply to backend type. If a backend block exists and is complete, Terraform may validate it. If backend selection is supplied by the execution environment, the absence of a backend block should not make the root module invalid.

#### Should saved plans record which backend type was used?

They can if Terraform Core has an internal reason to record that execution metadata.

The important distinction is that backend type is not part of the infrastructure graph being planned. The backend controls where Terraform state is stored and how state locking is performed during execution. It does not change the desired remote objects represented by the plan.

So if Terraform records backend type internally for diagnostics, provenance, or safety checks, that is fine. The proposal only argues that the root module source should not be the only place backend type can be selected.

#### Is changing from `-backend=azurerm` to `-backend=s3` a source change or an execution change?

It can be either, depending on the workflow.

For teams that intentionally declare the backend in the Terraform root module, changing backend type is naturally a source change.

For teams where backend selection is owned by CI/CD, wrappers, or deployment orchestration, changing backend type is an execution change. It may still live in source control, for example in `azure-pipelines.yml`, a GitHub Actions workflow, a Terragrunt wrapper, or another deployment orchestrator. But source-controlled execution configuration is not necessarily the same lifecycle as Terraform configuration.

This proposal is intended to support both models.

#### How should `.terraform/terraform.tfstate` track backend metadata?

It can continue tracking backend metadata the same way it does today.

Terraform already records initialized backend details under `.terraform`, which is local working-directory execution state rather than root module source. Selecting the backend type through `terraform init -backend=...` could feed that same internal mechanism.

The implementation detail does not need to change conceptually. The only difference is that backend type may come from the init command rather than from a backend block.

**How would wrappers such as HCP Terraform, Terraform Enterprise, Terragrunt, Atlantis, Azure Pipelines, and GitHub Actions reason about this?**

This can be introduced as an additive CLI feature.

Existing wrappers that rely on backend blocks would continue to work unchanged. Wrappers that want to own backend selection could opt in by passing `-backend=...`.

If a wrapper currently assumes backend type comes from Terraform configuration source, this feature would not break that assumption unless the wrapper chooses to use the new argument.

Many wrappers already treat backend initialization as execution context by providing backend settings, credentials, workspaces, variable files, and environment-specific state keys outside the root module. Allowing backend type to be passed at init time would give those workflows a more direct expression of what they already do.

#### What happens if two operators run the same source with different backend types?

That possibility already exists in practice, depending on the workflow.

Two operators can already run the same source with different backend coordinates by supplying different `-backend-config` values, credentials, workspaces, state keys, or generated backend files. The current requirement for a backend block does not fully prevent execution divergence; it mainly requires the backend adapter declaration to appear in the Terraform source.

For workflows that want to prevent divergence, declaring the backend block in source remains a valid option.

For workflows that intentionally allow execution-owned backend selection, using different backend types would be an explicit initialization decision.

If both a source-declared backend and `-backend` are present but disagree, Terraform should fail loudly with a clear diagnostic.

**Would this make backend changes too easy or unsafe?**

It should not, if treated consistently with existing backend initialization behavior.

Changing backend storage is already an explicit `terraform init` concern. Terraform already detects backend changes and asks for migration or reconfiguration behavior where appropriate.

The proposed feature would not silently change state. It would only allow the backend adapter type to be supplied by the same execution lifecycle that already supplies backend attributes.

Terraform could preserve existing safety checks around backend changes, migration prompts, and reconfiguration.

#### Does this remove support for backend blocks?

No.

Existing backend blocks would remain valid and continue to be the default pattern for users who want backend type declared in Terraform source.

This proposal only adds a second, explicit path for workflows where backend selection is owned by execution automation.


### References

- #38466

Related context: Terraform `1.15.0` introduced validation of backend block attributes that was incompatible with partial backend configuration supplied via `-backend-config`. Terraform `1.15.1` reverted that behavior. This proposal follows the same lifecycle boundary: backend initialization details can be execution context and should not require source configuration beyond what is actually part of the infrastructure model.
issues.title: Allow backend type to be selected during `terraform init` without requiring a backend block in configuration

### Use Cases

I have other usecases there but the simplest one I have is this:

I have a reverse proxy tool that is based on Tailscale and a Nomad cluster which I use Terraform to manage.

Each service has one .tf file and I prefer to have all the stuff related to a specific service on that service file, which may include
- The postgres database setup
- The reverse proxy entry
- Setup on the actual place it is going to run: nomad, vercel or cloudflare workers

On the reverse proxy entry, there are two main strategies:
- Traefik to expose to the world through the VPS: doable using the Nomad service annotation
- ts-proxy: Instance of ts-proxy on a nomad task

For organization, I keep all ts-proxy instances in one nomad job having each proxy for a service in it's own group. Implementation details, but there is a big variable in my svc_ts_proxy.tf, that, ideally, should be defined by parts on the services using it.

It's a dictionary where the key is the service name and the value has the node where the state volume is going to be created, the name of the nomad service being proxied, the hostname on Tailscale and the name of the state volume on Nomad 

### Attempted Solutions

- The god variable, that concentrates logic from many services into one place, so setting up a new service is not just creating one new file and touching only that file + template Nomad from that god variable (approach being used).
- Duplicating Nomad code for ts-proxy to use as a sidecar, gets too repetitive.
- Modules: each one would become a different Nomad job, would work but I think it gets too noisy on the dashboard

### Proposal

A way to declare a dict variable in one of the .tf files in the module and other files on that same module can attribute values on a key in this variable.

Example:
meta_tsproxy.tf: variable hosts as map[string]Settings, where Settings is the type declared on the variable
svc_foo.tf: hosts[foo] = {host = "whiterun", name = "foo"}
svc_bar.tf: hosts[bar] = {host = "whiterun", name = "bar"}

So the final value becomes those values in one dictionary readable by other .tf in the same module.
