issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.15.2
on linux_arm64
+ provider registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/random v3.7.2


Reproducible identically on `darwin_arm64` and `linux_amd64` — the code path that emits the diagnostic lives in core, not in any platform-specific shim.
```

### Use Cases

The canonical pattern for managing write-only secret values in Terraform — straight from the docs on ephemeral values — combines:

```hcl
ephemeral "random_password" "this" {
  length = 32
}

resource "aws_secretsmanager_secret" "this" {
  name       = var.name
  kms_key_id = var.kms_key_id
}

resource "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "this" {
  secret_id        = aws_secretsmanager_secret.this.id
  secret_string_wo = ephemeral.random_password.this.result
}
```

This shape gives the user three desirable properties at once: the random value never enters state, the secret is encrypted with a caller-supplied KMS key, and rotation is handled by bumping a `*_wo_version` integer. Wrapping it into a small helper module so multiple consumer modules can reuse it is the obvious next step.

Once that helper exists, consumers want to test that they wire it correctly. The most common security-relevant invariant is "the helper is invoked with the right `kms_key_id`" — easy to assert structurally if the test framework can plan / apply the consumer under `mock_provider`. Today it cannot. The first parse of the helper trips the diagnostic below, regardless of which assertion the test was going to make. Every downstream module that depends on the helper is uniformly untestable.

The pattern isn't niche: any module that surfaces a random-generated secret value (RDS master password, OAuth client credentials, OIDC cookie key, …) follows the same shape; the testing gap blocks all of them.

### Attempted Solutions

We tried, in order:

1. **Module-local tests** for the helper itself — `command = apply` with `mock_provider`. The error fires at module-load time, before any `run` block executes:
   ```
   Error: No ephemeral resource types in mock providers
     with ephemeral.random_password.this,
   The provider mocking mechanism does not yet support ephemeral resource
   types.
   ```
2. **Plan-only tests** — `command = plan`. Same diagnostic; the rejection isn't apply-specific.
3. **`override_module`** on the helper from the consumer module's tests:
   ```hcl
   override_module {
     target = module.helper
     outputs = { secret_arn = "arn:aws:secretsmanager:..." }
   }
   ```
   The module is still loaded for type-checking before the override applies, so the ephemeral block is still parsed and the diagnostic still fires. The override has no effect on the rejection.
4. **Variable-level validation tests** — `validation {}` blocks inside `variable "X"` are testable via `expect_failures` at `command = plan` because the variable is evaluated before the resource graph is walked. We use this for "is `kms_key_id` non-null" type invariants. But it cannot cover invariants that live on resource attributes (the actual `kms_key_id` value flowing into `aws_secretsmanager_secret`, downstream wiring of `secret_arn` into IAM grants, etc.) — those require an actual plan, which is what's blocked.
5. **Falling back to `make env.<env>.check`** against the real AWS provider on a host with credentials. Works, but moves the assertion from CI-friendly `terraform test` into an SSO-driven manual workflow, with the security-relevant invariants only checked by humans at PR-review time.

None of these close the gap for consuming modules that need to assert on resource-level attributes inside an ephemeral-using helper.

### Proposal

Extend `mock_provider` so ephemeral resource types follow the same model as managed resources:

- `mock_resource` blocks accept defaults for ephemeral types, returning the configured values from `OpenEphemeralResource` and the appropriate empty / no-op responses from `RenewEphemeralResource` and `CloseEphemeralResource`. Example:
  ```hcl
  mock_provider "random" {
    mock_resource "random_password" {
      defaults = {
        result = "mock-password-value"
      }
    }
  }
  ```
- `override_resource` blocks accept ephemeral resource addresses, overriding the mock defaults for a specific instance, same syntax as managed resources today.
- `ValidateEphemeralResourceConfig` returns no diagnostics under the mock provider, leaving validation to the consumer's own logic.

Concretely, in `internal/providers/mock.go`, the four ephemeral protocol methods today return the same hard-coded diagnostic; three carry a `FIXME: Design some means to mock an ephemeral resource type.` comment (introduced 2024-09-13 in `3b77e57ce4854820411134caf44361d48e75ce83`). Replacing those stubs with the same `Mock` / `Resources` / `Overrides` plumbing the managed-resource methods already use would close the gap symmetrically.

We do not have a preference between "default to a generated mock value of the correct type" vs. "require the user to set `mock_resource` defaults explicitly". The first is more ergonomic; the second is more predictable. Either is dramatically better than the current state, where no path through the test framework reaches the consuming module's resources.

### References

- `internal/providers/mock.go` — `FIXME: Design some means to mock an ephemeral resource type.` introduced in commit https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/commit/3b77e57ce4854820411134caf44361d48e75ce83 (2024-09-13). This is the closest thing to a tracking artefact for the work; a GitHub-issue search for "mock_provider ephemeral" / "No ephemeral resource types in mock providers" returns no issue or PR as of the date this request is filed.
- https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/commit/9c3dc8f73a21dcac28d754d9e556e4bbc5a1b60a — protocol-symbol rename adding `Resource` suffix (`OpenEphemeral` → `OpenEphemeralResource`, etc.); cleans the API surface around which a mock implementation would be written, but doesn't itself touch the mock stubs.
- https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/commit/c70a885afbd3827b72f26892b9fe6f156e3b9eb7 — adds `ValidateEphemeralResourceConfig` to the interface, completing the protocol surface for both the real and mock implementations.
- Related but distinct: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/38309 (open) — root-module `terraform validate` rejects ephemeral outputs. Different code path, but trips users in similar testing workflows and is worth tracking alongside.
- Unrelated to mocking but found during search, for completeness: hashicorp/terraform#35912 (panic on apply, fixed), #36518 (dynamic write-only + nested ephemeral, fixed), #37270 (`depends_on` on ephemeral resources).

This request was drafted with the help of Claude (Anthropic) in a Claude Code session; the reproducer, code references, and search-for-prior-art steps were verified manually against the linked commits and source.

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.15.x
```

### Use Cases


- **Quick Resource Lookup**: As a Terraform user, I often need to find specific resources in large state files without manually parsing JSON or using external tools like `jq`.

- **Debugging and Troubleshooting**: When debugging infrastructure issues, I need to quickly locate resources by type, name, or attribute values to understand the current state.

- **State File Navigation**: Large state files with hundreds of resources make it difficult to find specific resources without a dedicated search tool.

- **Attribute-Based Search**: There's no built-in way to search for resources based on their attribute values (e.g., finding all resources with a specific IP address or tag).

- **Improved Developer Experience**: A built-in search command would streamline workflows by eliminating the need to export state to JSON and use external tools for searching.

### Attempted Solutions

- **Manual JSON Parsing**: Used `terraform show -json` and manually searched through the output, which is time-consuming and error-prone for large state files.

- **External Tools**: Used `jq` or other JSON processors to search state files, requiring additional tool installation and complex query syntax.

- **terraform state list**: Used the existing `terraform state list` command, but it only lists resource addresses without search capabilities or attribute inspection.

- **terraform state show**: Used `terraform state show` to inspect individual resources, but this requires knowing the exact resource address beforehand.

### Proposal


# Introduce a new Terraform command: `terraform state find`

Key Features:
- **Search by Resource Type**: Find all resources of a specific type (e.g., `aws_instance`, `aws_s3_bucket`)
- **Search by Resource Name**: Locate resources by their name or partial name match
- **Search by Attribute Values**: Find resources containing specific attribute values (e.g., IP addresses, tags, IDs)
- **Flexible Matching**: Support both substring and exact matching with case-insensitive search by default
- **Multiple Output Formats**: Display results in human-readable text or JSON format for scripting

`terraform state find -h`

Usage: terraform state find [options] <keyword>

Search for resources in the Terraform state file by matching keywords
against resource addresses, types, and attribute values.

Options:
  -state=<path>          Path to the state file (default: auto-detected)
  -format=text|json      Output format (default: text)
  -exact                 Exact string match only (default: substring match)
  -ignore-case=true|false Case-insensitive search (default: true)

Examples:
  terraform state find aws_instance
  terraform state find my-resource-name
  terraform state find "10.0.0.1"
  terraform state find -exact web-server
  terraform state find -format=json security_group
  terraform state find -state=/path/to/state postgres

Additional Features:

- **Match Type Indication**: Show where the match was found (type, name, address, or attribute)
- **Attribute Field Highlighting**: When matching on attributes, display which field contained the match
- **Module Support**: Search across resources in both root and child modules
- **Comprehensive Results**: Display resource address, type, name, module path, and match details

Example Scenarios:

1. Search for a VPC by name:

```
terraform state find demo-vpc
```

Output:

```
Searching for 'demo-vpc' in state...
Found 1 resource(s):

=====================================

Address: ibm_is_vpc.main_vpc
  Type: ibm_is_vpc
  Name: main_vpc
  Match: attribute
  Matched Field: name
  Attributes: 33 field(s)

=====================================
Total: 1 resource(s) matched
```

2. Find all resources of a specific type:

```
terraform state find aws_instance
```

Output:

```
Searching for 'aws_instance' in state...
Found 3 resource(s):

=====================================

Address: aws_instance.web
  Type: aws_instance
  Name: web
  Match: type

Address: aws_instance.app[0]
  Type: aws_instance
  Name: app
  Match: type

Address: aws_instance.db
  Type: aws_instance
  Name: db
  Match: type

=====================================
Total: 3 resource(s) matched
```

3. Search for resources with a specific IP address:

```
terraform state find "10.0.1.5"
```

Output:

```
Searching for '10.0.1.5' in state...
Found 1 resource(s):

=====================================

Address: aws_instance.web
  Type: aws_instance
  Name: web
  Match: attribute
  Matched Field: private_ip
  Attributes: 15 field(s)

=====================================
Total: 1 resource(s) matched
```

4. Get JSON output for scripting:

```
terraform state find -format=json security_group
```

Output:

```json
{
  "results": [
    {
      "address": "aws_security_group.web",
      "type": "aws_security_group",
      "name": "web",
      "match_type": "type"
    }
  ],
  "count": 1
}
```

### References

- Related to state management improvements
- Complements existing `terraform state` subcommands
- Addresses common workflow pain points in state file navigation

When the `version` is evaluated to `null` I expected the `version` attribute to act as if it was not set. The [documentation for `null`](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/expressions/types#null) _seems_ to imply this should be the case:

> a value that represents absence or omission. If you set an argument of a resource to null, Terraform behaves as though you had completely omitted it — it will use the argument's default value if it has one, or raise an error if the argument is mandatory.

So, in this case, if `version` is evaluated to `null` I'd expect to be able to set `source` to a non-registry value.

### Actual Behavior

The actual behavior is that a `null` version constraint is [handled as a empty set constraint](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/terraform/node_module_install.go#L295-L299). This means that the version is treated as being set instead of omitted, which causes the `source` to be validated as a registry.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. `terraform init`

### Additional Context

I am very excited about the new dynamic module source feature! I _think_ this is a bug in how the version constraint is handled specifically for modules (the empty set constraint comment makes sense in other things that take versions, like providers) but maybe it is an enhancement?

The end goal of supporting this is both consistency with existing `null` behavior as well as the ability to make the `source` of a module flexible enough to point to different types of underlying systems.

This is a Request for Comments (RFC) regarding a proposed AI-mediated zero-trust handshake for Terraform.

## Background
Currently, Terraform establishes a plugin session using a magic cookie for initial handshake. However, as the ecosystem grows towards zero-trust architectures, there is a need for dynamic capability negotiation, rich workload identity (like SPIFFE JWT-SVID), and fine-grained, per-RPC authorization based on dynamic contexts (such as AI-driven anomaly detection on proposed resource graphs).

## Proposed Solution
We propose a minimalist, secure two-phase handshake approach that leverages existing gRPC interceptors and JWTs without the need for an over-engineered full gRPC proxy or stateful shadow handles. 

1. **New Handshake Protocol**: The core queries a local or external `AIGatekeeper` with an `AITripartiteHandshakeRequest` (containing `WorkloadIdentity`, structured `DAGPreview`, nonce, timestamp).
2. **Authorization JWT**: The Gatekeeper returns a signed JWT encapsulating permitted claims (`allowed_providers`, `allowed_resource_types`).
3. **gRPC Interceptor**: We introduce a `AIGatekeeperInterceptor` in the core that intercepts every RPC call, validates the JWT, and enforces the claims.
4. **Fallback Mode**: The feature is guarded by `TF_ENABLE_AI_MEDIATED_RPC` and gracefully degrades if the inference engine is unavailable.

Please see the attached Pull Request for a draft implementation of the revised protobufs and the gRPC interceptor logic. We welcome maintainer feedback.

### Use Cases

Terraform already documents its AI usage guidelines in CONTRIBUTING.md, including expectations around transparency, accountability, code quality, and the 🤖🤖🤖 PR title convention for AI-assisted contributions.

The problem is that many contributors using AI coding tools never see these guidelines before changes are generated. Most tools don't automatically read CONTRIBUTING.md, so repository-specific requirements are often missed and only become apparent after a pull request is opened.

Surfacing this guidance earlier in the contribution workflow would help contributors follow the project's expectations from the start, reducing avoidable review feedback while making the process smoother for both contributors and maintainers.

### Attempted Solutions

The AI usage guidance in `.github/CONTRIBUTING.md` already works well and should remain the canonical documentation for the project. The challenge is simply that many contributors using AI coding tools never see it before generating changes, since those tools don't automatically read `CONTRIBUTING.md`. As a result, repository-specific expectations are easy to miss and often only come up during code review, leading to unnecessary back-and-forth that could be avoided by surfacing the guidance earlier in the contribution workflow.


### Proposal

Add an `AGENTS.md` file at the repository root that mirrors the existing AI Usage section from `.github/CONTRIBUTING.md`.

The purpose of this file is to surface the existing guidance earlier for contributors using AI coding tools. It would **not** introduce any new policy.

Specifically, `AGENTS.md` would include:

* **Transparency**

  * Document the existing `🤖🤖🤖` PR title requirement for AI-assisted contributions.

* **Contributor responsibility**

  * Reinforce that contributors remain accountable for the code they submit, regardless of how it was generated.

* **Quality expectations**

  * Mirror the existing expectations around reviewing, validating, and taking ownership of AI-assisted changes before submission.

### Scope

* Keep `.github/CONTRIBUTING.md` as the **canonical** source of the AI usage policy.
* Add `AGENTS.md` as a discoverable copy of the same guidance for AI coding agents and contributors who use them.
* Introduce **no new policy** only improve when and how contributors encounter the existing guidance.


### References

- Existing AI Usage policy: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/.github/CONTRIBUTING.md#ai-usage
- AGENTS.md specification: https://agents.md/

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.15.7
on linux_amd64
```

### Use Cases

New contributors to Terraform Core currently need to manually set up their development environment by following the steps in CONTRIBUTING.md: installing the correct Go version (per .go-version), Git, protoc for `make protobuf`, and other tooling like `changie` for changelog entries.

This manual setup has a few problems:
- It's easy to end up with a mismatched Go version, since .go-version and go.mod specify different things (build version vs. minimum compatible version), and it's not obvious to a newcomer which one to actually install.
- Tooling like protoc isn't installable via `go get`, so contributors on different OSes each have to figure out their own installation path, leading to inconsistent local environments across contributors.
- CONTRIBUTING.md notes the project currently only targets Linux and Mac OS X for development due to Unix-specific assumptions in the test suite — Windows contributors have no clear supported path to a working environment.
- Environment drift between contributors' machines can cause "works on my machine" issues that are hard to debug and unrelated to the actual code change being reviewed.

The end goal is for any contributor — regardless of OS or local setup — to get a working, correctly-versioned Terraform Core development environment with a single step, reducing onboarding friction and eliminating environment-related inconsistencies in review.

### Attempted Solutions

I followed the manual setup steps in CONTRIBUTING.md:

- Checked .go-version vs. go.mod for the Go version to install — the doc doesn't make clear which one a new contributor should actually install locally.
- Ran `go install .` and `go test ./...` successfully after cloning outside GOPATH.
- Ran into friction with `make protobuf`, which needs `protoc` installed separately (not fetchable via `go get`), with no documented version to target.
- Noted the doc states dev is only supported on Linux/Mac OS X due to Unix-specific test assumptions — no documented path for Windows contributors (e.g. via WSL).

None of these block a determined contributor, but each step is a place where two people following the same doc can end up with different environments — none of it caused by their actual code changes.

### Proposal

Add a `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` (and associated Dockerfile if needed) to the repository, following the Dev Container spec (https://containers.dev/).

This would define:
- The correct Go toolchain version, sourced from .go-version
- protoc and any other Protocol Buffers tooling needed for `make protobuf`
- Git
- Node.js/npx, needed for `npx changie new`
- Any linters or formatters used in CI

Contributors using VS Code, GitHub Codespaces, or any other Dev Container-compatible tool could then open the repository and get a fully configured environment automatically, with no manual installation steps. This would also give Windows-based contributors a viable path to a working Linux-based dev environment via the container, addressing the current Linux/Mac-only limitation noted in CONTRIBUTING.md.

This is purely additive tooling — it wouldn't change the existing manual setup instructions or require anyone to adopt it, just offer an alternative for those who want a zero-config environment.

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.15.8
on windows_amd64
+ provider registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws v6.56.0
```

### Use Cases

When developing modules, it is often convenient to output one or more complete resources as output fields, instead of individual fields. This helps the module remain useful without needing consistent updates when fields are added or removed from individual resources.

For example, if I have a module that creates an S3 bucket and configures replication on it, it may contain:

`bucket.tf`
```
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
  bucket = "my-tf-test-bucket"

  tags = {
    Name        = "My bucket"
    Environment = "Dev"
  }
}

output "bucket" {
  value = aws_s3_bucket.example
}
```

This allows the user of the module to then access whatever fields on the bucket they like (e.g. `bucket_regional_domain_name`), and new fields added in new provider versions will be available without needing to modify the module.

A recent change (I'm not sure when exactly this changed, but it's an issue as of Terraform v1.15.8) has caused this to log deprecation warnings for every deprecated field on the resource in the `output`. In the example above, it will cause a deprecation warning like this:

```
Warning: Deprecated value used
│ 
│   on bucket.tf line 11, in output "bucket":
│   11:   value       = aws_s3_bucket.example
│ 
│   The deprecation originates from aws_s3_bucket.example.website_domain
│ 
│ website_domainis deprecated. [more deprecation instructions here]
│ 
│ (and 13 more similar warnings elsewhere)
```

### Attempted Solutions

My module now filters out all deprecated fields like so:

```
output "bucket" {
  description = "The `aws_s3_bucket` resource that was created."
  value = {
    for k, v in aws_s3_bucket.example :
    k => v
    if !contains(
      [
        "acceleration_status",
        "acl",
        "grant",
        "cors_rule",
        "lifecycle_rule",
        "logging",
        "object_lock_configuration",
        "policy",
        "replication_configuration",
        "request_payer",
        "server_side_encryption_configuration",
        "versioning",
        "website",
        "website_domain",
        "website_endpoint",
    ], k)
  }
}
```

But this is obviously not sustainable as it requires a new release of the module for every deprecation change.

### Proposal

Ignore deprecation warnings for `output` values. Or, if that's too broad, ignore deprecation warnings when an entire resource is being referenced and not an individual attribute.

### References

_No response_

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.17.0-dev
(behaviour described here is the same on v1.16.x and earlier)
```

### Use Cases

When reviewing a change to infrastructure, or onboarding someone onto an existing stack, the question people actually ask is architectural: *what does this system look like, and what talks to what?* Today Terraform can tell you the resources and their dependency order, but there is no first-class way to see the shape of the infrastructure being described.

Concrete situations where this comes up:

1. **Change review.** A plan touching 60 resources is reviewed as a wall of text. A reviewer wants to see that the change adds a subnet inside an existing VPC and repoints a load balancer, not to reconstruct that mentally from `+`/`~`/`-` lines.
2. **Onboarding and handover.** New joiners on an existing module set need the network/zone/subnet containment hierarchy. That information is fully present in the configuration and state, but has to be redrawn by hand into a diagram that then goes stale.
3. **Documentation that stays current.** Teams keep architecture diagrams in Confluence/`docs/` that drift from the real infrastructure within weeks, because nothing regenerates them from the source of truth.
4. **Design/compliance review.** Reviewers want to confirm that a database sits in a private subnet and is not routable from the internet — a containment and reachability question that reads naturally off a diagram.

### Attempted Solutions

`terraform graph` is the closest existing feature, and it is genuinely useful, but it answers a different question. It renders Terraform's internal dependency graph — evaluation order between nodes — in DOT or Mermaid:

```
terraform graph
terraform graph -type=plan -format=mermaid
```

That output is a dependency DAG keyed on Terraform addresses. It deliberately does not model infrastructure topology: there are no regions, VPCs, availability zones or subnets as containers, no notion that an ALB fronts an instance, and no distinction between "A must be created before B" and "A sends traffic to B". For a non-trivial configuration the resource-dependency graph is also large enough that it is hard to read as a picture of the system.

The other route is the JSON plan:

```
terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json
```

This is a documented, stable interface and it does carry the information needed. But every consumer then has to independently rebuild the same provider-specific knowledge — which attribute on `aws_instance` points at a subnet, that `google_compute_subnetwork` lives inside a VPC network, that `ip_configuration[0].subnet_id` is the Azure equivalent — before it can draw anything.

I have built one such consumer, [`tf-arch-diagram-generator`](https://github.com/mchittineni/tf-arch-diagram-generator) (disclosure: I am the author), which takes `terraform show -json` output and renders an architecture diagram for AWS, Google Cloud and Azure, with the containment hierarchy, inferred traffic flows and per-resource plan diffs. I mention it as evidence that the transformation is tractable from data Terraform already emits, not to propose it as the implementation.

### Proposal

The concrete gap is that architecture-level visualisation has no supported place in the workflow, so each tool re-derives provider semantics from scratch and the results are inconsistent.

There are a few directions, in increasing order of scope. I would be glad to be told that only the first is in scope for Terraform Core:

**1. Point people at the right interface (smallest).** Document in the `terraform graph` reference that it renders the dependency graph rather than an architecture diagram, and that `terraform show -json` is the intended interface for external visualisation. This is cheap and would save a lot of misdirected effort — `terraform graph` is what people reach for first, and it is not what they want.

**2. Make `terraform graph` readable as a picture.** Optionally group nodes into subgraphs by module in the Mermaid output, so that the existing command produces something legible for a medium-sized configuration:

```
terraform graph -format=mermaid -group=module
```

This stays entirely within Terraform's own model — no provider-specific knowledge — and is a much smaller change than anything below.

**3. A supported way to express containment (largest).** The reason external tools need per-provider heuristics is that nothing in the schema says "this attribute references a container this resource lives inside". If providers could advertise that (for example, a schema-level hint that `subnet_id` is a containment reference), any consumer of `terraform show -json` could build the hierarchy generically, and diagram tooling could stop hardcoding resource-type tables. This is clearly the most invasive option and would need provider-protocol design, so I raise it as the underlying problem rather than as a request.

I am not asking Terraform to render images. Option 1 alone would be a real improvement, and I am happy to open a PR for it.

### References

- `terraform graph` — existing dependency-graph rendering (DOT/Mermaid)
- `terraform show -json` — the documented machine-readable plan interface
- [mchittineni/tf-arch-diagram-generator](https://github.com/mchittineni/tf-arch-diagram-generator) — prior art demonstrating the transformation from `terraform show -json` (authored by me)
issues.title: Architecture-level visualization: terraform graph renders the dependency graph, not the infrastructure topology

This is a problem since github is introducing rate limits for unauthenticated requests even against public repositories, see https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/206581#discussioncomment-18269083

### Attempted Solutions

I can configure the module to check out a specific git repository and version instead of relying on the registry, e.g.
`source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/somemodule?ref=v1.0.0"`

I can override https://github.com to ssh://git@github.com, e.g. by running
`git config --global url."ssh://git@github.com/".insteadOf "https://github.com/"`.
Would probably work for CI environments, however I don't want to force colleagues to patch their local git configs as they might rely on https for other projects. Running terraform locally should, in my opinion, use the same checkout mechanism as in CI. I also think that a solution incorporated in terraform would be more elegant.

I can configure authentication for HTTPS git fetches, however I already have an SSH key at hand and would like to use a single authentication method everywhere.

`module "some_bucket" {
  source = "terraform-aws-modules/s3-bucket/aws"
  git_fetch_mode = "ssh|https"
  ...
}
`

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.17.0-dev
on darwin_arm64
```

### Use Cases

I run Terraform drift checks on a schedule and in CI, across a lot of workspaces. I want them to fire only when something has actually changed outside of Terraform, and to never be able to change anything themselves.

Detection isn't the missing piece, though it's fiddly. `terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode` already returns exit `2` only when there's drift (an unapplied config change doesn't trigger it), and `-json` emits `resource_drift`, but you have to know that exact flag combination and parse the JSON to see what actually changed. Two bigger things are the problem.

First, I can't tell a check to ignore drift I already know about, just for that run. There's always some noise, like a tag a scanner rewrites every hour or an attribute the provider keeps normalizing. My only knob today is `ignore_changes`, and it's the wrong tool for an alarm (more on that below). So I either get paged for noise or mute the whole resource and miss real drift on it.

Second, the check isn't guaranteed read-only. I'm running `plan`, which takes `-out` and is one step from something appliable. I'd be a lot more comfortable scheduling that across dozens of workspaces, or handing it to compliance, if it simply couldn't change anything.

### Attempted Solutions

For finding drift the refresh-only route is fine.

```
terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode          # 2 on drift, 0 otherwise
terraform plan -refresh-only -json | jq '[.. | select(.type? == "resource_drift")]'
```

It's the suppression part that breaks down. Take that scanner rewriting `tags["LastScanned"]` every hour, so every run lights up on it. Right now I have two options.

- Put `ignore_changes = [tags["LastScanned"]]` in the config. That quiets the alarm, but now `apply` won't reconcile that tag either, it needs a review, and it's global, not scoped to this one check.
- Filter the `-json` in `jq` and work out the exit code myself. That's a fragile script I have to babysit per resource type.

Neither lets me ignore that one tag for this check while still failing on any other drift.

I also looked at `terraform refresh`, but it does the opposite of what I need here. It writes the drifted values into state, which erases the very drift I'm trying to detect.

### Proposal

I'd propose a `terraform drift` command. What makes it more than a wrapper around `plan -refresh-only` is a `-ignore` flag that hides expected drift from the report, and only the report.

`terraform drift -ignore=aws_s3_bucket.demo` drops a whole resource; `-ignore='aws_instance.web:tags["LastScanned"]'` drops one attribute. The address is just the normal resource instance address you already use in plan output and `-target` (count/for_each and modules work, managed resources only), and the attribute part is the same syntax as `ignore_changes`. It only affects what's printed, never state, never infra, never what a later plan or apply does. If it can't apply a rule cleanly, it shows the full drift instead, and anything it hides is still counted and labeled. It only masks what you name, so if the same resource drifted somewhere else you still see it and the check still fails. That's the one thing the refresh-only plus `jq` route can't do without a config change, and it's the part I've built.

The command itself is small.

```
terraform drift          # human-readable report
terraform drift -json    # adds a drift_summary with counts
```

A few specifics.

- It's strictly read-only. It forces refresh-only and rejects `-destroy` and `-refresh=false` (without a refresh it would report "no drift" regardless of the real state), and it can't apply or destroy under any arguments, which a `plan`-based check can't promise.
- Exit codes are `0` no drift, `1` error, `2` drift. The `2` lines up with what `plan -detailed-exitcode` already means. There's no "drift plus pending config" case to worry about, since refresh-only never looks at config changes, and if the refresh itself falls over that's just an error (`1`).
- In `-json` the only new thing is a `drift_summary` message with `changed`/`deleted`/`total`/`ignored`. `resource_drift` is the existing message, untouched.

`terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode -json` already handles detection and gives a clean exit code, so this isn't about finding drift. It's about being able to suppress expected drift per run, and having one read-only command to reach for instead of that flag combination.

On scope, in case it matters for the decision, this is a CLI-layer change with nothing touched in Terraform Core or the backends. I'll share the full diff when there's a PR.

On shape, the real alternative is hanging `-ignore` (and a drift-scoped exit code) off `plan -refresh-only` instead of a new command, and honestly I'd be fine with that. The catch is `plan` still can't promise read-only (it takes `-out`) and its flag list is already long. Changing what `plan -detailed-exitcode` returns is off the table, since it'd break everyone relying on today's `0`/`1`/`2`.

I've got a working implementation with tests and I've run it against a real AWS provider, so I'm glad to share the branch. But per the contributing guide I wanted to talk about direction before dropping code. The real question is do you want a read-only drift command with a suppression flag at all, or would you rather the suppression be a flag on `plan -refresh-only`? Since `-ignore` is the whole reason for the command, I'd put it in v1, though I'm happy to stage its surface (resource-level first, attribute-level as a follow-up) if you'd prefer something smaller to start.

### References

- #28803 (closed, addressed by #30486): the drift-report noise problem; #30486 de-noised the plan view, `-ignore` is the per-run lever for a standalone check.
- #35226 (open): asks that `plan` exit `0` when everything matches, showing demand for drift-scoped exit semantics.
issues.title: A first-class `terraform drift` command for detecting infrastructure changed outside of Terraform

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.15.4
```

### Use Cases

Many organizations require resource metadata such as tags or labels to reflect the last modification performed through Terraform.

Common examples include:

- modified-datetime
- last-updated
- updated-by
- change-ticket
- deployment-reference

Today Terraform can set those values during resource creation, but it has no native mechanism to update them automatically when a resource is modified.

This makes governance, auditing and operational tracking difficult, especially in large environments where thousands of resources are managed through Terraform.

The end goal is to allow users to automatically update metadata whenever Terraform detects a resource change and applies an update.

### Attempted Solutions

Several approaches were evaluated:

### Using timestamps
```
tags = {
  modified-datetime = timestamp()
}
```

This causes perpetual diffs because the timestamp changes on every plan.

### Using external data sources
``` 
data "external" "git_date" {
  program = ["bash", "-c", "git log -1 --format=%cs"]
}
```

This only reflects repository state and not actual Terraform resource updates.


### Using null_resource triggers
```
resource "null_resource" "metadata" {
  triggers = {
    modified_datetime = timestamp()
  }
}
```
This does not provide a way to update attributes of another resource before it is modified.

###Using lifecycle
```
lifecycle {
  ignore_changes = [
    tags["modified-datetime"]
  ]
}
```

This avoids drift but prevents Terraform from managing the value.

None of these approaches provide a generic and reliable mechanism to update resource metadata only when a resource is actually modified.


### Proposal

Introduce a lifecycle hook executed immediately before a resource update operation. 
Example: 
```
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "example" {
   bucket = "my-bucket"
   tags = { 
       Environment = "prod" 
    } 
  lifecycle { 
      before_update { 
            tags = merge(self.tags, { modified-datetime = timestamp() }) }
     } 
}
```

### References

Related discussions: 
- Support for resource lifecycle hooks 
- Support for update-time metadata tracking 
- Common requests around automatic tagging and auditing

 I was unable to find a Terraform Core feature that currently addresses this requirement.
issues.title: Feature Request: Lifecycle pre-update hook for resource metadata modification

issues.body:
We rely on `terraform validate` as a quick check for reusable modules and their submodules before publishing them. Adding `deprecated` to an output now makes that check fail, even though the output is valid when the module is called by another module.

Could `validate` take an option that tells it we're checking a reusable module rather than a deployment root? We'd like to keep running validation directly against each module without removing deprecation declarations or building a wrapper just to make the check run.

This is related to [hashicorp/terraform#39207](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/39207), which covers the same restriction during `terraform test`. This request is specifically about keeping the standalone `terraform validate` check available.

## Terraform version

```text
Terraform v1.16.2
on windows_amd64
```

No providers, credentials or cloud resources are needed for this example.

## Reproduction

`main.tf`:

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.15.0"
}

variable "name" {
  type       = string
  default    = "example"
  deprecated = "This input is kept for compatibility."
}

output "old_name" {
  value      = var.name
  deprecated = "This output is kept for compatibility."
}
```

Run from the module directory:

```powershell
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
```

Validation exits with code 1:

```text
Error: Root module output deprecated

  on main.tf line 13, in output "old_name":
  13:   deprecated = "This output is kept for compatibility."

Root module outputs cannot be deprecated, as there is no higher-level module to inform of the deprecation.
```

Removing only the output's `deprecated` line makes validation pass. The input variable can remain deprecated. The hard failure here is the root-only restriction on the output, not an error caused by the deprecated input variable.

## Requested behavior

An explicit option such as `terraform validate -reusable-module` would let us say that this directory is intended to be called as a child module. The flag name is just a suggestion; a narrower option for the deprecated-output restriction would also help.

With that option, `validate` should accept deprecated outputs that are valid in a reusable module, retain any applicable deprecation warnings, and still fail on invalid syntax, bad references, type errors, invalid arguments and other genuine validation errors. The existing behavior should remain the default for normal root configurations, and this should not change `plan` or `apply`.

This isn't a request for a general "ignore errors" switch. We want the validation checks, without a failure that comes solely from treating a reusable module as a deployment root.

## Why this matters

The documentation describes `validate` as being "primarily useful for general verification of reusable modules": https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/validate

Validating examples is useful too, but it only checks modules that those examples actually reference. A separate check against each module directory is valuable, including for submodules that don't yet have an example. Writing wrappers also means supplying inputs and provider wiring just to run a static check.

I understand from [hashicorp/terraform#38309](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/38309) that `validate` currently expects a complete root configuration, and that changing this may involve more than one output validation rule. That issue covers the similar problem with ephemeral outputs. An explicit reusable-module option would make the intended context clear without quietly changing how existing configurations are checked.
issues.title: Allow terraform validate to check reusable modules with deprecated outputs

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.18.0-dev
```

### Use Cases

In large enterprise Terraform deployments (1,000 to 5,000+ resources, modules, and providers), executing `terraform plan` and `terraform apply` allocates significant heap memory during Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) walks in `internal/dag/walk.go`.

Profiling large graph walks (`pprof` & `b.ReportAllocs()`) reveals that graph execution creates ~18–20 heap object allocations per node every time `Walker.Walk()` runs. On a 2,500-node graph, a single walk allocates ~5.8 MB of RAM across 50,457 separate heap allocations.

Reducing these redundant memory allocations improves overall CLI throughput and decreases memory pressure on execution environments with memory constraints (such as CI/CD runners, Terraform Cloud / Enterprise worker agents, and local developer machines).

### Attempted Solutions

We profiled the `Walker.Walk` engine in `internal/dag/walk.go` across Linear, Diamond, and Grid graph topologies and identified 3 key sources of unnecessary allocations:

1. **Map Re-allocation**: `w.vertexMap`, `w.diagsMap`, `w.upstreamFailed`, and `info.deps` are initialized without capacity hints, causing Go to re-allocate internal hash tables as vertices are added.
2. **Redundant Map Duplication**: In `Walk()`, `info.deps` was stored as `map[Vertex]chan struct{}`. Because Go maps are invariant, passing `info.deps` to `waitDeps(..., map[Vertex]<-chan struct{})` forced a manual map creation (`make(map...)`) and key-by-key copy loop for every node in `g.edgesFrom`.
3. **Dummy Channel Allocations for Root Nodes**: For nodes without dependencies (`info.DepsCh == nil`), `walkVertex` allocated a dummy channel (`make(chan bool, 1)`), wrote `true` to it, and closed it just to satisfy the `select` statement.

### Proposal

We propose 3 non-breaking internal optimizations in `internal/dag/walk.go`:

1. **Pre-allocate map capacities** using `g.vertices.Len()` hints for `vertexMap`, `diagsMap`, and `upstreamFailed`, and `depsSet.Len()` for `info.deps`.
2. **Update `walkerVertex.deps` type to `map[Vertex]<-chan struct{}`**. This enables implicit channel type-casting on map insertion and allows passing `info.deps` directly into `go w.waitDeps(...)` with **zero map allocations and zero copy loops**.
3. **Directly evaluate root node dependencies**: Replace dummy channel allocations with an `if info.DepsCh != nil` check in `walkVertex`.

### Benchmark Metrics (`go test -bench=BenchmarkWalker_Walk -benchmem ./internal/dag`)

| Topology Scenario | Metric | Baseline (Before) | Proposed (After) | Net Improvement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Linear Graph (1,000 nodes)** | Time / Memory | 4.14 ms / 2.26 MB | **3.23 ms / 1.69 MB** | **⚡ 22.0% faster / 25.4% less RAM** |
| **Linear Graph (1,000 nodes)** | Allocs / op | 18,158 allocs | **14,229 allocs** | **⚡ 21.6% fewer allocs** |
| **Diamond Graph (1,000 nodes)** | Time / Memory | 6.60 ms / 2.70 MB | **4.14 ms / 2.00 MB** | **⚡ 37.2% faster / 25.8% less RAM** |
| **Diamond Graph (1,000 nodes)** | Allocs / op | 20,937 allocs | **17,345 allocs** | **⚡ 17.1% fewer allocs** |
| **Grid Mesh (2,500 nodes)** | Time / Memory | 11.64 ms / 5.83 MB | **8.92 ms / 4.72 MB** | **⚡ 23.3% faster / 19.0% less RAM** |
| **Grid Mesh (2,500 nodes)** | Allocs / op | 50,457 allocs | **43,332 allocs** | **⚡ 14.1% fewer allocs** |

I have benchmarked this change locally, verified all `internal/dag` unit tests pass (`PASS`), and can submit a PR if the core maintainers are open to reviewing it.

### References

- N/A
issues.title: performance/dag: reduce memory allocations and improve graph walk execution speed by ~25%

I was annoyed with how slow `terraform init` is, so I went looking for bugs in the provider installer. This is one I found, AI-assisted.

When a provider is linked from the global plugin cache and the lock file has checksums for it, the installer reads and hashes the whole cached package three times. I have a small fix to `internal/providercache/installer.go` that hashes it at most once and reuses the result. It leaves the lock file checks themselves (#32129) unchanged. For the configuration below it takes `terraform init` from 1.28s to 0.50s wall time and from 0.99s to 0.35s CPU time (median of 8 runs, Apple silicon Mac). I'd like to open a PR for it if that's welcome.

### Terraform Version

```
Terraform v1.16.3
on darwin_arm64
```

Also reproduces on `main` (78194be60).

### Terraform Configuration Files

```terraform
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "6.44.0"
    }
  }
}
```

### Debug Output

Not attached. The trace log has no lines for the hashing itself, only a gap before `providercache.Dir.LinkFromOtherCache: linking registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws`.

### Expected Behavior

The cached package is read and hashed once.

### Actual Behavior

The same package is hashed three times during `EnsureProviderVersions`, and each pass reads the whole package (770MB for `hashicorp/aws` 6.44.0):

1. `installer.go:426`: `cached.MatchesAnyHash(preferredHashes)` checks the cache entry against the lock file.
2. `dir_modify.go:66`: `LinkFromOtherCache` checks the same hashes again before linking.
3. `installer.go:540`: `cached.Hash()` computes the hash again for the lock file update.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Save the configuration above as `main.tf`, with a plugin cache enabled: `export TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR=$HOME/.terraform.d/plugin-cache`.
2. `terraform providers lock -platform=darwin_arm64 -platform=linux_amd64`
3. `terraform init` once, to fill the plugin cache.
4. Copy `main.tf` and `.terraform.lock.hcl` into an empty directory and run `time terraform init` there.

### Additional Context

It only happens with the global plugin cache enabled and a lock file that has checksums for the provider. Without a lock file entry, the cache entry is only used with `plugin_cache_may_break_dependency_lock_file` set, and is then hashed once.

### Generative AI / LLM assisted development?

Claude Code (Claude Opus 5). I used it to find the problem and to write this issue text.
issues.title: terraform init hashes a cached provider package three times when linking it from the plugin cache

issues.body:
While looking at why `terraform init` is slow, I found that it never reuses a connection to the provider registry.

`RegistrySource` builds a new `http.Client`, with its own connection pool, for every request. So each provider's version lookup and each package metadata request opens a new TCP connection and repeats the TLS handshake. The mirror source next door (`NewHTTPMirrorSource`) already keeps one client for its lifetime, so the fix is to do the same in `RegistrySource`. I have a patch ready and would like to open a PR if that's welcome.

### Terraform Version

```
Terraform v1.16.3
on darwin_arm64
```

Also reproduces on `main` (78194be60).

### Terraform Configuration Files

```terraform
terraform {
  required_providers {
    null   = { source = "hashicorp/null", version = "3.3.2" }
    random = { source = "hashicorp/random", version = "3.9.1" }
    local  = { source = "hashicorp/local", version = "2.9.0" }
    time   = { source = "hashicorp/time", version = "0.13.1" }
    http   = { source = "hashicorp/http", version = "3.6.1" }
  }
}
```

### Debug Output

Not attached. The trace log shows each `/versions` request taking about one round trip longer than a request on an established connection.

### Expected Behavior

Requests to the same registry host reuse a connection, as they do for a network mirror.

### Actual Behavior

Each request opens a new connection. `registryClient()` (`registry_source.go:147`) ends with `newRegistryClient(url, creds)`, which calls `httpclient.New()` and so builds a fresh `http.Transport` every time. The client is used for one request and dropped, so its connection pool is never reused.

A test against an `httptest` server confirms it: two `AvailableVersions` calls for providers on the same host open two connections.

For the configuration above, with a lock file and a warm plugin cache, so the only traffic is discovery plus five version lookups:

| Round-trip latency to the registry | Stock | Patched |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ~6ms (CDN edge nearby) | 0.37s | 0.30s |
| +30ms, added by a local proxy | 1.05s | 0.64s |
| +150ms, added by a local proxy | 3.64s | 1.96s |

(median of 5 runs each, Apple silicon Mac)

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Save the configuration above as `main.tf`, with a plugin cache enabled: `export TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR=$HOME/.terraform.d/plugin-cache`.
2. `terraform providers lock`
3. `terraform init` once, to fill the plugin cache.
4. Copy `main.tf` and `.terraform.lock.hcl` into an empty directory and run `time terraform init` there, watching connections with `tcpdump` or `lsof`, or against a proxy that adds latency.

### Additional Context

The effect scales with the number of providers and with the distance to the registry, so it is most visible on a slow link or from a region far from the CDN edge.

There is more to gain on the download side, which this covers none of. Package downloads build their own client per provider, so each zip opens a connection to a host the installer has usually just used for `SHA256SUMS`; and providers are installed strictly one after another, so an `init` costs the sum of every provider's round trips and transfer time rather than the longest of them. They interact, so I have not prepared a patch for either. I would rather hear from a maintainer on whether that direction is wanted, and in what shape, before writing one.

### Generative AI / LLM assisted development?

Claude Code (Claude Opus 5). I used it to find the problem and to write this issue text.
issues.title: terraform init opens a new TCP connection for every provider registry request

### Terraform Version

### Terraform Version

Terraform v1.16.4

### Use Cases

When reviewing a terraform plan, I want to know which Terraform resource an unknown argument refers to before approving the apply.

For example, a security group can be configured with vpc_id = aws_vpc.example.id. When the VPC is being created in the same plan, the security group's vpc_id is displayed as (known after apply). The AWS VPC ID cannot be known yet, but the Terraform reference aws_vpc.example.id is already known from the configuration.

### Example configuration
- main.tf
```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region                      = "ap-northeast-1"
  access_key                  = "test"
  secret_key                  = "test"
  skip_credentials_validation = true
  skip_metadata_api_check     = true
  skip_requesting_account_id  = true
  endpoints {
    ec2 = "http://kumo:4566"
  }
}
resource "aws_vpc" "example" {
  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
  tags = {
    Name = "plan-reference-example"
  }
}
resource "aws_security_group" "example" {
  name        = "plan-reference-example"
  description = "Demonstrates an unknown value from a resource reference"
  vpc_id      = aws_vpc.example.id

  tags = {
    Name = "plan-reference-example"
  }
}
```
- versions.tf

Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

This VPC example is intentionally simple. In a large plan with many resources, however, seeing only (known after apply) makes it difficult to tell which resource an argument refers to. I would like the plan itself to show that reference so it can be reviewed without tracing it through the configuration.

### Attempted Solutions

I ran terraform plan with the configuration shown above. The security group's vpc_id appeared as (known after apply), without indicating that its value comes from aws_vpc.example.id.

I can find the reference by inspecting the Terraform configuration, but I could not find an existing option to display it in the human-readable plan output. I have not tried another workaround.

### Proposal

For arguments whose value is unknown because they reference another Terraform resource, show the source reference in plan output.

Current output:
```bash
+ vpc_id = (known after apply)
```
Proposed output (example):
```bash
+ vpc_id = (known after apply; from aws_vpc.example.id)
```

issues.body:
### TL;DR
State can silently hold two addresses bound to one remote object. When that happens, `terraform plan` shows a routine-looking `destroy` that actually targets live infrastructure, with no hint that the object is also tracked elsewhere. An earlier ID-based duplicate check was deliberately relaxed (#33390 → #33434) because raw import IDs are not a sound uniqueness key — but resource identity (v1.12+) is exactly that key, and HCP Terraform already uses it in its bulk-import workflow to detect objects managed by another workspace. I propose bringing the same detection into core, within a single state: warn at plan time when two managed instances share an identity, and at import time when the imported object is already tracked.

### Use Cases

A real incident:

1. An AWS Secrets Manager secret was bound to a root-level address, likely via an old ad-hoc `terraform import` or a local apply of uncommitted config.
2. The same secret is properly managed by a module instance (`module.app.aws_secretsmanager_secret.rds_password`). State ended up with two entries pointing to one remote object.
3. The root-level address had no configuration, so `plan` proposed a `destroy`. Applying it would have scheduled deletion of the live secret referenced by running ECS tasks.
4. Nothing in the plan output indicated the duplication. A human reviewer caught it by noticing the name collision.

Duplicate tracking commonly arises from CLI `import` to a second address, local applies of never-merged config, or module refactors that import into the new address without removing the old entry. The resulting destroy diffs are indistinguishable from legitimate ones.

The import documentation states the assumption but nothing enforces it:

> Terraform expects that each remote object it is managing will be bound to only one resource address. (...) If you import the same object multiple times, Terraform may exhibit unwanted behavior.

### Current Behavior

- `plan` performs no duplicate detection across state entries.
- CLI `terraform import` performs no check against existing state.
- Config-driven import validates only duplicate *target addresses* among `import` blocks: [`internal/configs/module.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/configs/module.go) emits `"Duplicate import configuration for %q"` when two blocks share a `to` address. An earlier ID-based duplicate check was deliberately relaxed in #33434 (closing #33390), on the grounds that raw ID strings are not unique: abstract resources such as `time_sleep` legitimately return identical import responses for distinct instances, and as noted there, "Terraform cannot enforce any uniqueness in resources" from the ID alone.
- HCP Terraform uses resource identities in its bulk-import workflow "to determine when resources are managed by another workspace" ([bulk import docs](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import/bulk)). The detection capability exists; it is not applied within a single state in core.

### Proposal

Resource identity (v1.12+) resolves the objection that led to relaxing the earlier check. Unlike a raw ID string, an identity is provider-defined with a documented uniqueness contract: it "must correspond to at most one remote object per provider" ([identity docs](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/framework/resources/identity)). Core already persists it per instance: `ResourceInstanceObject.Identity` is serialized into state as `IdentityJSON` with `IdentitySchemaVersion` ([`internal/states/instance_object.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/states/instance_object.go)). So the data needed for comparison is already in state.

1. **Plan time (primary):** warn when two managed instances of the same resource type in the same state share an identity, naming both addresses. This catches pre-existing duplicates — like the incident above — exactly when a reviewer is looking at the dangerous destroy.
2. **Import time:** apply the same check when an `import` block or CLI `terraform import` targets an object whose identity matches an existing managed instance.

Scope the check to resource types whose provider defines an identity schema, and skip the rest. That avoids re-introducing the #33390 false positives by construction: abstract resources like `time_sleep` have no meaningful remote identity and would simply not participate. Defaulting to a warning rather than a hard error keeps intentional workflows (e.g. deliberate co-management patterns) working, while making the documented assumption visible when violated. A flag could opt into an error.

### Attempted Solutions

- Process discipline (only reviewed `import` blocks, no local applies). This does not catch duplicates already present in state.
- External audit in CI: `terraform state pull | jq`, grouping instances by `(type, id)`. This works, but every team reinvents it, and raw string IDs are exactly what #33434 established as unsound — and what resource identity was introduced to improve on.

### Terraform Version

n/a — feature request; behavior confirmed against v1.16 documentation and current `main` source.

### References

- [Import docs warning](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/import) — "bound to only one resource address"
- #33390 / #33434 — the earlier ID-based duplicate check among `import` blocks and why it was relaxed to a `to`-address check
- [`internal/configs/module.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/configs/module.go) — current duplicate-`to` validation; [`internal/states/instance_object.go`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/main/internal/states/instance_object.go) — identity persisted in state
- [Resource identity concepts](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/framework/resources/identity) — implementable in both the [Plugin Framework](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/framework/resources/identity) and [SDKv2](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/sdkv2/resources/identity), so coverage extends to legacy-SDK providers
- [Bulk import](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import/bulk) — HCP's cross-workspace detection via identity
- #29160 — related: auto-import of existing resources matching configuration
issues.title: Use resource identity to detect two state entries tracking the same remote object

issues.body:
### Terraform Versions and Benchmark Results

The aggregate `self` lookup path is present in Terraform v1.16.5 and v1.17.0-beta2: `internal/lang/eval.go` resolves `self` through `GetResource`, and `internal/terraform/evaluate.go` decodes all instances for that resource.

I ran the aggregate-resolution benchmark with 128 `for_each` instances (five runs; median shown). It calls `evaluationStateData.GetResource` directly, matching the aggregate path used by `self`. These are focused evaluator microbenchmarks, not end-to-end plan measurements. The temporary baseline-only harness was adapted from the fixture in PR #39328; it does not measure the targeted implementation.

| Terraform tag | Median ns/op | B/op | allocs/op |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| v1.16.5 | 911,679 | 991,735 | 13,117 |
| v1.17.0-beta2 | 779,313 | 890,137 | 11,708 |

Environment: Linux/amd64, Go 1.27.1, AMD Ryzen 7 255 with Radeon 780M Graphics.

For context, PR #39328's separate `main` benchmark reported about 961 µs / 13,246 allocations for aggregate resolution versus 10.7 µs / 136 allocations for targeted instance resolution. Those figures were measured on a different code revision and toolchain, so they are not directly comparable to the tag results above.

### Use Cases

Configurations with many `count` or `for_each` instances can evaluate lifecycle postconditions that refer to the current instance through `self`. In that context, only the addressed instance is needed. Resolving the containing resource and decoding all siblings for each `self` reference can add work that grows with the number of instances, even though the condition is per-instance.

### Attempted Solutions

Issue #26355 and PR #37154 addressed broader costs in high-cardinality resource evaluation, but did not address this specific `self` lookup path. PR #39328 explored a targeted instance lookup and added regression coverage for `count`, `for_each`, sensitive values, missing indices/holes, planned values, pending deletion, and sibling isolation. It was closed before technical review because the required proposal discussion had not happened first.

### Proposal

Before another implementation PR, would the Terraform Core maintainers be open to reviewing a narrowly-scoped optimization so a per-instance `self` reference can resolve only its addressed instance, while preserving existing behavior for missing instances and other aggregate references? If this is not the right direction, guidance on the preferred design or whether this case is in scope would be appreciated. I’m happy to adjust or drop the implementation based on that feedback.

### References

- #26355 — Performance issues when referencing high cardinality resources
- #37154 — reduce instance change lookups in GetResource
- #39328 — closed PR with the proposed implementation and benchmark
issues.title: Improve performance of per-instance `self` references with count/for_each

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.9.x
AWS Provider v5.x (latest)
```

### Use Cases

We manage our MWAA environments with Terraform. We need to upgrade from Airflow 2.11.x to 3.x. Amazon MWAA now supports native in-place major-version upgrades (with an automatic metadata-DB snapshot and rollback), but the aws_mwaa_environment resource still forces a destroy/recreate when the major version changes. This means Terraform deletes the existing environment and its metadata database instead of performing the in-place upgrade the service now supports, which is unacceptable for production environments.


### Attempted Solutions

Upgrading to the latest hashicorp/aws provider does not help — the ForceNew-on-major-version logic is still present in the current provider code:

customdiff.ForceNewIf("airflow_version", func(...) bool {
    return oldVersion.Segments()[0] < newVersion.Segments()[0]
})

The only working path today is to upgrade out-of-band (console / aws mwaa update-environment), set lifecycle { ignore_changes = [airflow_version] }, and then reconcile Terraform state so it doesn't plan a replacement.


### Proposal

Update aws_mwaa_environment so a supported major-version upgrade is applied in-place via the UpdateEnvironment API rather than triggering ForceNew. The ForceNewIf guard was originally added to work around issue #21640, where the MWAA API rejected major upgrades. That limitation no longer applies now that MWAA supports in-place major-version upgrades, so the guard is outdated.


### References

- Original (now-outdated) issue that introduced the ForceNew: #21640
- MWAA in-place version upgrades: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/introducing-in-place-version-upgrades-with-amazon-mwaa/
- MWAA upgrading an environment: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mwaa/latest/userguide/upgrading-environment.html

### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.16.6
on darwin_arm64
```

### Use Cases

AWS WAF byte match rules can apply an `MD5` text transformation to a request component before comparing it with `SearchString`. Writing such a rule requires the comparison value to be the Base64 encoding of the raw 16-byte MD5 digest.

Terraform's `md5` function returns a hexadecimal string. `base64encode(md5(value))` encodes the ASCII hexadecimal representation, not the raw digest bytes. The existing `base64sha256` and `base64sha512` functions provide the required behavior for their respective algorithms, but there is no MD5 equivalent or general conversion function.

This differs from converting between two provider arguments. The value is derived from arbitrary input and must match a transformation performed by the remote service.

### Attempted Solutions

The closest expression using built-in functions is:

```hcl
base64encode(md5(var.value))
```

This Base64-encodes the hexadecimal digest rather than the raw digest bytes.

A shell workaround is:

```shell
printf '%s' "$INPUT" | openssl dgst -md5 -binary | openssl base64 -A
```

Using this from Terraform requires an external data source, provider-defined function, or another out-of-process step. This adds dependencies and execution overhead for a deterministic transformation.

### Proposal

Provide a built-in way to return the Base64 encoding of raw MD5 digest bytes.

One option is a `base64md5` function, consistent with `base64sha256` and `base64sha512`:

```hcl
base64md5("hello world")
```

Alternatively, a general function that directly transcodes hexadecimal data to Base64 would allow composition without introducing binary strings:

```hcl
base64_from_hex(md5("hello world"))
```

The exact API name is open for discussion. In either form, the result would be:

```text
XrY7u+Ae7tCTyyK7j1rNww==
```

### References

- #19245 requested `base64md5` and was closed in favor of provider-side conversion.
- #26163 requested hex-to-binary conversion and was closed after its original provider-specific use case was resolved.
issues.title: Support Base64 encoding of raw MD5 digest bytes

## Terraform Version

v1.17.0

## Use Cases

Terraform creates a new evaluation scope for each block it evaluates, and each scope derives its own table of built-in functions. Nearly all of that table depends only on the working directory, yet it is built again from scratch — about 43 µs and 526 allocations per block. The cost scales with the number of blocks rather than the size of the plan, so a configuration with many resources, locals, outputs or module calls pays it thousands of times on every `plan`, `apply`, `validate` and `test`.

Measured against unpatched Terraform 1.17.0 on the same host; medians, with repetitions:

| Run (repetitions) | Baseline | CPU | Wall-clock |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `terraform validate`, large module (20) | 2.93 CPU-s, 1.34 s | −17.9% | −12.0% |
| `terraform plan`, 1,900 resource changes (15) | 10.72 CPU-s, 5.14 s | −9.1% | −5.1% |
| `terraform test -json -verbose`, large schemas (6) | 50.92 CPU-s, 26.70 s | −9.4% | −4.8% |
| `terraform test`, human output (10) | 19.70 CPU-s, 13.72 s | −3.7% | −0.3% |

## Attempted Solutions

None — the cost is internal to Terraform; the example branch linked below implements the proposed approach.

## Proposal

Build the entries that depend only on the base directory once per base directory and share them read-only. Each scope copies the shared table and replaces the ~15 entries that depend on its other settings: the filesystem and template functions, `type` and `plantimestamp`, the pure-only wrappers, and functions contributed by providers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph current["today"]
    C1["each evaluated block"] --> C2["new scope"] --> C3["build the whole function table"]
  end
  subgraph proposed["proposed"]
    P1["each evaluated block"] --> P2["new scope"] --> P3["copy the shared table"] --> P4["replace scope-dependent entries"]
    P0["first block for a base directory"] --> P5["build the shared table once"] --> P3
  end
```

Behaviour is unchanged: every scope keeps its own map with the same names, descriptions, parameters and results, and scope-dependent entries are still computed from that scope's own settings on its first call. A test compares the table against the previous algorithm across 256 scope configurations, with separate tests for base directories, prior-result checking, templating and concurrent use.

An example implementation, with tests and benchmark, is in a fork: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/compare/main...andrewesweet:terraform:fm/tf-perf-scope-functions

## References

No duplicate found (searched open and closed issues and pull requests with several phrasings, 25 Oct 2026).

An LLM agent drafted this issue and the change on that branch. The human submitter has reviewed both, can explain them, and owns them.

## Terraform Version

v1.17.0

## Use Cases

### Problem

When `terraform test` runs with `-json -verbose`, every run block's `test_plan`
or `test_state` message embeds the complete provider schemas in its
`provider_schemas` attribute — an identical payload repeated once per run
block. With mainstream providers this attribute is 92–98% of all bytes written
to the stream. Terraform pays to marshal and encode it after every run block;
every consumer pays to read, transfer and often strip it. This is the
documented machine-readable form that CI reporters and tools consume.

### Evidence

Unpatched v1.17.0 built the same way as the patched build, one host, medians:

| Run | Baseline median | With `-no-provider-schemas` | Reps |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `terraform test -json -verbose`, large provider schemas (7 files, 93 run blocks; large cloud providers, mocked) | 26.704 s wall / 50.923 CPU-s | −12.6% wall, −6.9% CPU, peak RSS 215→187 MiB | 6 |
| `terraform test -json -verbose`, small provider schemas (12 files, 56 run blocks) | 13.771 s wall / 19.749 CPU-s | no change | 10 |
| `terraform plan` / `terraform validate` / human-output `terraform test` | 5.143 s / 1.340 s / 13.718 s wall | no change; the option does not apply | 15 / 20 / 10 |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph today["Today, per run block"]
    direction LR
    R1["run block 1"] -->|"test_plan / test_state with full provider_schemas"| C1["consumer"]
    R2["run block 2"] -->|"the same provider_schemas again"| C1
  end
  subgraph proposed["With -no-provider-schemas (opt-in)"]
    direction LR
    R3["run block 1"] -->|"test_plan / test_state without provider_schemas"| C2["consumer"]
    R4["run block 2"] -->|"the same, no provider_schemas"| C2
  end
```

## Attempted Solutions

No existing flag omits these schemas; consumers today must read, transfer and strip the repeated payload.

## Proposal

### Proposed change

A new opt-in `-no-provider-schemas` option on `terraform test` (requiring
`-json`; rejected with `-cloud-run`, where a local flag cannot change the
remote stream): `test_plan` and `test_state` omit the `provider_schemas`
attribute when it is set. An alternative — emit each schema once per
invocation instead of per run block — helps every consumer but changes the
documented message shape, so the patch takes the backward-compatible route;
this issue asks which shape you prefer. The option name is a maintainer
question.

### Behaviour preservation

Default output is byte-identical: a characterisation test pinned the current
behaviour (complete schemas on every run block's message) before the change
and passes after; exact-message tests pin that both message types are
otherwise unchanged; measured results, plans and states are identical apart
from the omitted attribute.

Intent to implement: **yes**. Example branch (placeholder until pushed):
https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/compare/main...andrewesweet:terraform:fm/tf-perf-test-schemas

## References

No existing issue reports this cost (searched 24–25 Oct 2026); related but
different: #33878, #35759.

The human submitter has reviewed both, understands every line, and owns them.

## Terraform Version

v1.17.0 and current `main`.

## Use Cases

Terraform routes Go's standard-library `log` package through its logging set-up
(`internal/logging`) so that `log.Printf` messages participate in `TF_LOG` level
filtering, `TF_LOG_PATH` capture and JSON formatting. When logging is disabled —
the default, and likewise `TF_LOG=off` — each message is still fully processed:
`log.Printf` formats it, the hclog standard writer infers a level from the prefix
and copies the string, and only then is the entry discarded at the logger's level
check. Every ordinary `plan`, `apply`, `validate` and `test` invocation pays it; the
cost scales with the providers in a configuration and compounds for CI pipelines,
wrapper tooling and repeated `terraform test` runs.

## Measured impact

Measured end-to-end against unpatched 1.17.0 (control byte-identical to the
official release; medians; the build differed only in this change):

| Invocation (reps) | Baseline CPU, median | CPU | Wall-clock |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `terraform validate` (20) | 2.925 CPU-s | −6.6% | −8.3% |
| `terraform plan` (15) | 10.715 CPU-s | −6.6% | −7.2% |
| `terraform test -json -verbose`, large schemas (6) | 50.923 CPU-s | −4.8% | −4.4% |
| `terraform test` (10) | 19.699 CPU-s | −1.9% | −1.0% |

CPU savings of 3.4% or more never overlap the control's min–max range. A
microbenchmark of one discarded `log.Printf` call drops from 306 ns and one
allocation to 2 ns and none.

## Attempted Solutions

None — the cost is internal to Terraform’s logging wiring; the example branch linked below implements the proposed change.

## Proposal

While the global logger's level is `Off` and no sink is registered, point the
standard-library logger at `io.Discard` instead of the hclog standard writer.
Go's `log` package skips all formatting when a logger's output is exactly
`io.Discard`, so discarded messages cost close to nothing. One change at the
single wiring point; no call sites change, and every enabled configuration keeps
its current wiring. Implemented, with tests, on the example branch:

https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/compare/main...andrewesweet:terraform:fm/tf-perf-log-discard

### Behaviour preservation

Registered sinks receive every entry at every level regardless of the logger's
level — crash-log capture depends on this — so the change is sink-aware: while a
sink is registered the standard logger keeps its hclog wiring and the sink
continues to receive standard-log messages, while the primary output stays
silent. A sink registration rewires the standard logger before the sink starts
receiving, so no line is dropped in between. Crash and panic output does not
use the standard logger.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph current ["Current (logging disabled)"]
        direction LR
        A["log.Printf"] --> B["format message"] --> C["hclog writer: infer level, trim, copy"] --> D["level check: Off"] --> E["discarded"]
    end
    subgraph proposed ["Proposed (logging off, no sinks registered)"]
        direction LR
        F["log.Printf"] --> G["io.Discard: no formatting"]
    end
```

## References

No duplicate found (searched open and closed issues and pull requests with several phrasings, 25 Oct 2026).

## Disclosure

This issue and the example change were drafted by an LLM coding agent. The human
submitter has reviewed both and owns them, and will answer questions about them and
maintain the change.
issues.title: Standard-library log messages are formatted even when logging is disabled
