## Terraform Version

Terraform 1.17.0 (`018a99c83`), compared with the same release plus the prototype. Both use the same Go 1.26.10 release-build recipe on Linux/amd64.

## Use Cases

Module authors use several run blocks to test different inputs, assertions, and overrides against one configuration. `terraform test` builds and walks a validation graph before every run, even when the configuration and provider instances are unchanged. This repeats work that does not depend on run variables or state and increases local and CI feedback time.

## Attempted Solutions

A prototype caches validation results within each test file. Two existing suites ran without credentials, using mocked providers. Ten interleaved runs per binary on a four-core Linux host produced these medians for `terraform test -json -no-color`:

| Suite | Validation walks | Wall seconds, baseline → prototype | CPU seconds, baseline → prototype |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Azure regions](https://github.com/Azure/terraform-azurerm-avm-utl-regions/tree/66f5052aecfad44aca17d482795d8288da6ea5df), 56 runs in 12 files | 56 → 12 | 13.811 → 10.778 | 19.845 → 15.039 |
| Azure platform module, 93 runs in 7 files | 93 → 14 | 22.351 → 17.622 | 46.781 → 32.173 |

Wall time fell by 22.0% and 21.2%. CPU, including provider processes, fell by 24.2% and 31.2%. The baseline and prototype ranges do not overlap. Validation-walk counts come from separate untimed trace runs. Every run passed with identical outcomes and diagnostic content after excluding timestamps, elapsed times, and message ordering. These measurements do not establish a saving for every suite.

## Proposal

Validate each loaded configuration and provider mapping once per file, with a once-per-pair guard for parallel runs. Attach the result to every matching run, including errors. Keep planning, overrides, mocks, and cleanup unchanged. No command-line option is needed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Current
    A[Every run] --> B[Validate] --> C[Attach diagnostics]
  end
  subgraph Proposed
    D[Every run] --> E[Validate once per configuration/provider pair]
    E --> F[Attach diagnostics to every run]
  end
```

Command tests preserve serial diagnostic content and order, statuses, and human/JSON output. Parallel checks preserve diagnostic multisets and per-run attribution. Surprisingly, baseline parallel human diagnostics already interleave, so byte order is not stable. Independent repeated validation also checks that shared connection configuration remains unchanged.

Example branch: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/compare/main...andrewesweet:terraform:fm/tf-perf-test-validate

## References

- https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/36459
- https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/issues/34009

AI assistance: an AI coding assistant prepared the prototype, measurements, and this draft. The human submitter has reviewed this issue and the example change and owns them.

## Terraform Version

The source paths occur in Terraform 1.17.0 (`018a99c83`) and the local main baseline (`9ec49e06a`, 1.18.0-dev).
The measurements compare Terraform 1.17.0 with and without the proposed change, built identically with Go 1.26.10 on Linux/amd64.

## Use Cases

Large configurations pay for graph rendering and debug arguments during ordinary `terraform plan` and `terraform validate`, even with logging disabled. Graph construction sorts and renders whole graphs for trace messages. Reference analysis also builds lists of node names for debug messages. Go evaluates these arguments before the logging implementation can discard them. Avoiding this work can reduce command latency without changing configuration, providers, or planning behavior.

## Attempted Solutions

Disabling `TF_LOG` and leaving `TF_GRAPH_TRACE` unset does not prevent argument construction. On a four-core Linux host, a synthetic configuration with 1,000 `terraform_data` blocks produced these medians over 20 interleaved runs per binary:

| Command | Baseline wall / CPU | With guards wall / CPU | Reduction wall / CPU |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `plan` | 0.862 / 1.663 s | 0.751 / 1.529 s | 12.9% / 8.1% |
| `validate` | 0.248 / 0.505 s | 0.223 / 0.469 s | 10.5% / 7.2% |

Wall-time ranges overlap. In an existing Azure platform module with 87 resource blocks, full `validate` and an offline plan targeting one random-password resource showed negligible benefit: under 0.5% in wall time and CPU. Full cloud plans were not measured. The module's 93-run mocked test suite finished 5.1% faster and used 4.1% less CPU over ten interleaved runs per binary, with nonoverlapping ranges. These results do not establish a general saving.

## Proposal

Guard graph rendering in `BasicGraphBuilder` and `graphTransformerMulti` at trace level. Guard the name lists and per-edge debug arguments in `ReferenceTransformer` at debug level. The level check must account for registered log sinks, which can consume messages independently of `TF_LOG`.

The current and proposed paths differ only when no output consumes the message:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Current graph operation] --> B[Build log arguments] --> C[Logger filters message]
  D[Proposed graph operation] --> E{Output consumes level?}
  E -->|Yes| F[Build same arguments and log]
  E -->|No| G[Skip log arguments]
```

Graph operations and diagnostics remain unchanged. Subprocess tests pin complete messages for debug, trace, JSON, `TF_LOG_CORE`, `TF_GRAPH_TRACE`, and registered sinks. Plan/validate outputs match byte for byte. Test outcomes and diagnostics match after ignoring message order.

Example branch: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/compare/main...andrewesweet:terraform:fm/tf-perf-graph-profile

## References

- https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/pull/37155 identifies graph string generation as a performance cost and introduces `TF_GRAPH_TRACE`.

### Terraform Version

Terraform v1.17.0 on darwin_arm64 (also seen on 1.16.6 on linux_amd64)

### Terraform Configuration Files

```hcl
variable "n" { default = 500 }

locals {
  users = { for i in range(var.n) : "u${i}" => i }
  pairs = { for i in range(var.n) : "p${i}" => { member = "u${i}" } }
}

resource "terraform_data" "slow" {
  for_each = { for k, v in local.pairs : k => v if contains(keys(local.users), v.member) }
  input    = each.value
}
```

### Expected Behavior

A no-op plan of n instances takes time roughly linear in n.

### Actual Behavior

The resource expansion evaluates the for_each expression once, but then every instance evaluates the whole expression again to get its own `each.key`/`each.value`. With an expression that itself costs O(n), plan time grows with n squared or worse. No-op `terraform plan` of the configuration above:

| n | wall | user CPU |
|---|---|---|
| 250 | 5.6s | 17.6s |
| 500 | 22.4s | 139.2s |

Moving the same expression into `locals { x = ... }` and using `for_each = local.x` gives the identical plan in under a second.

We hit this in a configuration with ~12,000 instances, where most grant resources filter a ~850-entry map in their for_each. A no-op plan took 12-25 minutes, CPU-bound in Terraform core (the provider used under 10% of the CPU). Goroutine dumps taken during the plan showed almost all busy goroutines in:

```
NodePlannableResourceInstance.managedResourceExecute
  -> evaluateForEachExpression
  -> forEachEvaluator.ResourceValue
  -> forEachEvaluator.Value
  -> hclsyntax.(*ForExpr).Value
```

Moving the expressions into locals brought that plan down to 4-7 minutes with an identical result.

The per-instance evaluations are in `managedResourceExecute` (internal/terraform/node_resource_plan_instance.go), again in `plan()` and `planDataSource()` (node_resource_abstract_instance.go), and similarly in the apply walk (node_resource_apply_instance.go).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. `terraform init`
2. `terraform apply -auto-approve`
3. `time terraform plan`

### Additional Context

The instance expander already holds the repetition data that the resource expansion registered, and `node_resource_ephemeral.go` already uses `GetResourceInstanceRepetitionData` for this. I have a small patch that takes `each.key`/`each.value` from `ctx.InstanceExpander()` when the resource's expansion is known and not deferred, and falls back to evaluating the expression otherwise. With it, `go test ./internal/terraform/ ./internal/instances/` passes, and the plan above takes 0.5s at n=500 with identical output. If needed I can open a PR if this approach is acceptable.

Possibly related: #26355, #32937.

<details>
<summary>Patch (against v1.17.0)</summary>

```diff
diff --git a/internal/instances/expander.go b/internal/instances/expander.go
index a0f7ae43a..d9279cb30 100644
--- a/internal/instances/expander.go
+++ b/internal/instances/expander.go
@@ -1100,3 +1100,21 @@ func (e *Expander) ActionInstanceKeys(addr addrs.AbsAction) (keyType addrs.Insta
 	}
 	return exp.instanceKeys()
 }
+
+// KnownResourceInstanceRepetitionData is like GetResourceInstanceRepetitionData
+// but returns false instead of unknown data or panicking when the resource's
+// expansion is not registered, unknown or deferred.
+func (e *Expander) KnownResourceInstanceRepetitionData(addr addrs.AbsResourceInstance) (RepetitionData, bool) {
+	e.mu.RLock()
+	defer e.mu.RUnlock()
+
+	parentMod, known := e.findModule(addr.Module)
+	if !known {
+		return RepetitionData{}, false
+	}
+	exp, ok := parentMod.resources[addr.Resource.Resource]
+	if !ok || expansionIsDeferred(exp) {
+		return RepetitionData{}, false
+	}
+	return exp.repetitionData(addr.Resource.Key), true
+}
diff --git a/internal/terraform/eval_for_each.go b/internal/terraform/eval_for_each.go
index e6eb4535c..680ce9441 100644
--- a/internal/terraform/eval_for_each.go
+++ b/internal/terraform/eval_for_each.go
@@ -10,6 +10,7 @@ import (
 	"github.com/zclconf/go-cty/cty"
 
 	"github.com/hashicorp/terraform/internal/addrs"
+	"github.com/hashicorp/terraform/internal/configs"
 	"github.com/hashicorp/terraform/internal/instances"
 	"github.com/hashicorp/terraform/internal/lang/langrefs"
 	"github.com/hashicorp/terraform/internal/lang/marks"
@@ -425,3 +426,17 @@ func markSafeLengthInt(val cty.Value) int {
 	v, _ := val.Unmark()
 	return v.LengthInt()
 }
+
+// resourceInstanceRepetitionData returns each.key, each.value and count.index
+// for a resource instance, reusing the resource's expansion when available
+// instead of re-evaluating for_each once per instance.
+func resourceInstanceRepetitionData(ctx EvalContext, addr addrs.AbsResourceInstance, config *configs.Resource) instances.RepetitionData {
+	if data, ok := ctx.InstanceExpander().KnownResourceInstanceRepetitionData(addr); ok {
+		return data
```

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.17.1
on darwin_arm64
```

### Use Cases

Often, I have a use case where a module released in github is tied to a specific version of related code, for example a docker image, or a binary, an artifact, stored outside of github, and indexed by the release version. 
I can implement some workarounds, but it would be more elegant to be able to get this information within the context of a module, the same way path.module can provide the path to the module folder.

### Attempted Solutions

Currently: 
- I could parse the modules.json file to retrieve the module ref, and use it to get the artifact and deploy the service. This does not work anymore with terraform 1.15, because terraform init now would fail to find the modules.json file, because the ordering of init changed. This post is related to this (quite hacky) solution, which was working until terraform 1.15 https://discuss.hashicorp.com/t/how-can-i-reference-a-modules-source-within-the-module/5416
- I could pass the ref of the module in both the source of the module _and_ another field I could use within the module. But that creates possible inconsistencies, and seems redundant



### Proposal

Introduce the source module... Same as the path module, which allows to get path.root, path.module, path.cwd, but this source module would containt information about the module source.

- source.module would contain the source string
- source.ref would contain the evaluated ref of the module
- source.version would contain the version field of the module declaration


Examples
```
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "= 6.0.1"
}
# source.module would be "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws", source.version would be "= 6.0.1" and source.ref "6.0.1"

module "mymodule" {
  source  = "github.com/terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-vpc?ref=6.0.1"
}
# source.module would be "github.com/terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-vpc?ref=6.0.1", source.version would be "" and source.ref "6.0.1"
```

issues.body:
## Terraform Version

v1.17.0

## Use Cases

`terraform test` launches each provider again for every test file, including providers behind `mock_provider` blocks. These providers remain unconfigured, but each process repeats its startup and initialization work. Module authors commonly split scenarios across files and mock cloud providers to run tests without credentials. For those suites, process startup grows with the number of files rather than the number of distinct providers.

Two real Azure module suites ran without credentials on a four-core Linux host. Each configuration ran 10 times in alternating order. The baseline was unpatched Terraform 1.17.0, with both builds using Go 1.26.10 and identical release flags. The command was `terraform test -json -no-color`, using each module's own test directory. Times are medians, and CPU includes provider processes:

| Suite | Files / passing tests | Plugin launches, baseline → reuse | Wall seconds, baseline → reuse | CPU seconds, baseline → reuse |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Region-data utility | 12 / 56 | 36 → 3 | 13.826 → 12.919 (−6.6%) | 19.812 → 18.769 (−5.3%) |
| Platform module | 7 / 93 | 28 → 4 | 22.120 → 18.500 (−16.4%) | 46.244 → 41.798 (−9.6%) |

## Attempted Solutions

The plugin cache avoids downloads, not these repeated launches.

## Proposal

The proposed change keeps one unconfigured instance per mocked provider address for the test suite, then closes it after the last file. Each file retains its own mock data and overrides. Configured providers retain their per-file lifetime. An exited shared process is relaunched when another file needs it. No configuration option is added.

The arrows show provider use, not parallel file execution:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Current
    A[File A mock] --> P1[Process A]
    B[File B mock] --> P2[Process B]
  end
  subgraph Proposed
    C[File A mock] --> P[Shared unconfigured process]
    D[File B mock] --> P
  end
```

Pass/fail results and diagnostic content matched across all 80 timed invocations, including additional verbose runs. Tests also cover per-file mock isolation and configured-provider isolation. Provider-internal state across validation calls remains a review concern. Provider-defined function instances are outside this change.

The submitter intends to implement this and has an example branch ready: https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/compare/main...andrewesweet:terraform:fm/tf-perf-provider-reuse

## References

No duplicate found (searched open and closed issues and pull requests with several phrasings, 2 Nov 2026).

An LLM agent (Claude) wrote this patch. The submitter has reviewed every line and is responsible for it.

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.18.0-dev
on darwin_arm64
```

Built from `main` at 7cf2eaf. I have only verified this on `main`. From reading the code, the S3 backend has built one credential chain per `Configure` call since it moved to `aws-sdk-go-base` v2, but I have not tested older releases.

### Terraform Configuration Files

N copies of this block (the repro below generates 40), one per `terraform_remote_state` data source. Credentials come from the instance metadata service (IMDS):

```terraform
data "terraform_remote_state" "s1" {
  backend = "s3"
  config = {
    bucket = "tf-test"
    key    = "state-1/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "us-west-2"
  }
}
```

The repro points `ec2_metadata_service_endpoint` and `endpoints.s3` at local fakes, so no AWS account is needed.

### Debug Output

A self-contained reproduction, with a fake IMDSv2 server that counts client connections and a fake S3 that always answers `NoSuchKey`, is in this gist: https://gist.github.com/hugo-barros/d270b9de6bb84cd2188e543115f3049d

Results for 40 `terraform_remote_state` data sources (every data source then fails with `error loading the remote state: Unable to list objects in S3 bucket "tf-test"`, because the fake S3 has no objects; this is expected and identical in both runs):

| terraform | `-parallelism` | max simultaneous open IMDS connections | IMDS token requests | IMDS credential fetches |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `main` @ 7cf2eaf | 1 | **40** | 40 | 40 |
| `main` @ 7cf2eaf | 10 | **40** | 40 | 40 |
| proposed change (see below) | 1 | **1** | 1 | 1 |
| proposed change (see below) | 10 | **1** | 1 | 1 |

### Expected Behavior

Resolving identical credentials for N identical backends should not hold N connections to the metadata service open, or fetch the same credentials N times. The number of IMDS connections should not grow with the number of `terraform_remote_state` data sources.

### Actual Behavior

Each `terraform_remote_state` data source leaves one keep-alive connection to IMDS open (and performs a full token + credential round trip). `-parallelism=1` does not help, because the connections accumulate rather than overlap.

This matters where the metadata service limits concurrent connections. I hit this in a sandboxed microVM-based CI runner where the guest could hold at most about 30 concurrent connections to its metadata service. A workspace with more than 40 remote state data sources got exactly 30 successful credential resolutions, and every later `Configure` failed with the following, even though the plan otherwise completed:

```
Error: No valid credential sources found

Please see https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/backend/s3
for more information about providing credentials.

Error: failed to refresh cached credentials, no EC2 IMDS role found, operation error ec2imds: GetMetadata, failed to get API token, operation error ec2imds: getToken, exceeded maximum number of attempts, 3, request send failed, Put "http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token": dial tcp 169.254.169.254:80: i/o timeout
```

The ~30 limit is specific to that environment. On plain EC2 the visible effect is only the N redundant token and credential requests, plus N idle connections held for the transport's idle timeout.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Download `fakeaws.go` and `repro.sh` from the gist (requires Go and a `terraform` binary; no AWS account).
2. `./repro.sh /path/to/terraform 40 1`
3. Read `max_open` in the output. Try `./repro.sh /path/to/terraform 40 10` as well.

### Additional Context

**Where the connections come from**

1. Every `terraform_remote_state` creates its own `Backend` and calls `Configure`, which calls [`awsbase.GetAwsConfig`](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/7cf2eaf/internal/backend/remote-state/s3/backend.go#L1088) every time.
2. `aws-sdk-go-base` builds a new `awshttp.BuildableClient` per call unless [`Config.HTTPClient` is set](https://github.com/hashicorp/aws-sdk-go-base/blob/v2.0.0-beta.72/aws_config.go#L351), which the backend never does.
3. The IMDS client derives its own copy of that client in [`resolveHTTPClient`](https://github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/blob/feature/ec2/imds/v1.18.20/feature/ec2/imds/api_client.go#L281). [`clone()`](https://github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/blob/v1.41.5/aws/transport/http/client.go#L91) uses [`GetTransport()`](https://github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/blob/v1.41.5/aws/transport/http/client.go#L145), which returns `Transport.Clone()`, so the IMDS client owns a private connection pool inside the credentials provider.

Consequences: nothing in the backend can call `CloseIdleConnections` on that pool, and simply sharing one `BuildableClient` between backends would not share it either (it is cloned again). Passing a plain `*http.Client` via `Config.HTTPClient` would bypass `aws-sdk-go-base`'s proxy, CA bundle and `insecure` handling, and the IMDS client's fail-fast dial and header timeouts. I could not find an existing issue about this.

**Possible fixes (feedback requested)**

- **A. Share the resolved `aws.Config` between backends with identical settings.** Working implementation: https://github.com/hugo-barros/terraform/tree/s3-backend-share-resolved-aws-config. The cache key is a hash of every `awsbase.Config` field plus the whole process environment; concurrent callers share one in-flight resolution; failures are never cached; configs that cannot be keyed reliably are never shared. Trade-offs: it is a process-wide cache; later `Configure` calls no longer emit `aws-sdk-go-base`'s "Retrieved credentials" debug lines; and shared config/credentials file contents are only read on the first resolution (their paths, via the environment, are part of the key). It also removes the redundant token and credential requests.
- **B. In `aws-sdk-go-base`, create the IMDS client explicitly with keep-alives disabled** (keeping its fail-fast timeouts). That is smaller and sits at the layer that owns the problem, and would also help `terraform-provider-aws`. It would not remove the redundant credential fetches.

They are not mutually exclusive. Which direction would the team prefer? Per CONTRIBUTING I am not opening a PR until the team has had a chance to weigh in.

**Testing of A so far**

- New unit tests cover: identical configs share one resolution; every config field and the environment produce separate resolutions; failures are not cached; concurrent callers resolve once; uncacheable configs are never shared; a guard test fails if a dependency bump adds a field the key cannot represent; and backends configured with different credentials never receive each other's. They pass with `-race`, and I checked they fail when the cache is deliberately broken.
- The package's existing tests pass. The acceptance tests were not run (they need AWS).
- Unrelated: on unmodified `main`, two `TestBackendConfig_Proxy` subtests fail if `NO_PROXY`/`no_proxy` is set in the environment running the tests.

### References

None found. The repro and analysis above are the only references.

### Generative AI / LLM assisted development?

Yes. I used an LLM coding assistant (opencode) to investigate, to write the reproduction and the proposed patch, and to draft this report. The numbers above come from running the real binaries, and the unit tests were run with `-race`.
issues.title: S3 backend: every terraform_remote_state keeps its own connection to the instance metadata service open (N data sources => N open connections)

issues.body:
### Terraform Version

```shell
Terraform v1.18.0-dev (main branch)
```

### Use Cases

Terraform's dependency model works well for describing dependencies between resources in their desired steady state, but it cannot adequately describe dependencies between specific lifecycle operations required to safely transition from one valid state to another.

A common example occurs when resource A currently references resource B, and a configuration change simultaneously:

1. Updates A to remove the reference to B.
2. Destroys B.

For example, the initial configuration might be:

```hcl
resource "example_container" "a" {
  child_ids = [example_child.b.id]
}

resource "example_child" "b" {
  # ...
}
```

The desired configuration becomes:

```hcl
resource "example_container" "a" {
  child_ids = []
}

# example_child.b has been removed
```

Many infrastructure APIs enforce referential integrity and require the update to A to complete before B can be deleted.

The required transition is:

```text
A.update
   |
   v
update completes
   |
   v
B.destroy
```

However, the desired configuration no longer contains the reference from A to B that previously established the dependency.

Terraform can therefore plan both changes but execute the destroy before the update:

```text
B.destroy
   |
   v
A.update
```

The remote API can then reject deletion because B is still referenced by A.

This pattern occurs with many infrastructure APIs that enforce referential integrity. Examples reported with AWS include:

- Updating a CloudWatch composite alarm before destroying a metric alarm it previously referenced.
- Updating a WAFv2 Web ACL before destroying an IP set it previously referenced.
- Updating an ENI before destroying a security group previously associated with it.
- Updating an ElastiCache replication group before destroying its previous parameter group.

The end goal is for Terraform to be able to represent and enforce dependencies between the individual operations required to transition between two desired states, including relationships such as:

```text
A.update -> B.destroy
```

rather than being limited to a dependency relationship between A and B as resources.

This should remain fully declarative. Source-code ordering should not become significant, and users should not need to manually sequence multiple Terraform applies to express a valid infrastructure transition.

### Attempted Solutions

The existing Terraform dependency and lifecycle mechanisms do not appear to provide a general way to express this relationship.

### Implicit dependencies

In the original configuration, an expression such as:

```hcl
child_ids = [example_child.b.id]
```

allows Terraform to infer:

```text
A depends on B
```

However, the configuration change that requires the transition removes that reference.

The new desired configuration therefore no longer contains the relationship that is relevant to safely transitioning from the old state to the new state.

### `depends_on`

An explicit dependency can represent a hidden dependency between resources:

```hcl
resource "example_container" "a" {
  child_ids = []

  depends_on = [
    example_child.b
  ]
}
```

However, the required relationship is not simply:

```text
A depends on B
```

The required relationship for this transition is specifically:

```text
A.update -> B.destroy
```

Resource dependencies can require different ordering depending on the lifecycle operation being performed.

For example:

```text
B.create  -> A.create
A.update  -> B.destroy
A.destroy -> B.destroy
```

A single resource-level dependency cannot unambiguously express all of these relationships.

The problem becomes even more apparent when B is being removed entirely from the configuration.

### `create_before_destroy`

`create_before_destroy` controls replacement sequencing for a resource.

It does not express the general relationship:

```text
Complete an in-place update to A before beginning destruction of B.
```

The problem also occurs when B is being permanently removed rather than replaced.

### Reduced parallelism

Reducing Terraform parallelism does not solve the problem.

The requirement is not simply that the operations happen serially. The dependency graph must guarantee the specific ordering:

```text
A.update -> B.destroy
```

Serial execution in the opposite order would still fail.

### `-target`

`-target` can sometimes be used operationally to force portions of a transition to occur separately.

However, this does not represent the dependency in the Terraform configuration or execution graph. It moves the transition semantics into an external procedure.

The desired result is for Terraform to represent the complete valid transition in one plan and enforce it during one apply.

### Multiple applies

This transition can sometimes be accomplished by updating A in one Terraform apply and removing B in a subsequent apply.

That moves lifecycle ordering outside Terraform's declarative dependency graph and into an external deployment procedure.

The final desired configuration already describes the target infrastructure state. The missing capability is the ability to describe or derive the operation dependency required to safely transition to that state.

### Proposal

Terraform should support dependencies between specific planned lifecycle operations rather than representing all dependency semantics solely as relationships between resource instances.

Conceptually, Terraform's execution graph should be capable of representing edges such as:

```text
A.create   -> B.create
A.update   -> B.destroy
A.destroy  -> B.update
A.destroy  -> B.destroy
A.replace  -> B.update
```

The most immediate use case is:

```text
A.update -> B.destroy
```

### Operation-level dependency graph

Terraform already plans individual actions such as create, update, replace, and destroy.

The dependency graph should be capable of expressing ordering constraints between those planned operations.

For example:

```text
Previous configuration:

A ----references----> B


Desired configuration:

A (reference to B removed)

B (removed)


Planned operations:

A UPDATE
B DESTROY


Required operation graph:

A.update.complete
        |
        v
B.destroy.start
```

The exact HCL representation is less important than supporting this semantic in Terraform Core.

### Possible configuration syntax

One possible approach would be to extend lifecycle configuration with an operation-specific constraint.

For example, conceptually:

```hcl
resource "example_container" "a" {
  child_ids = []

  lifecycle {
    before_destroy_of = [
      example_child.b
    ]
  }
}
```

This could produce an execution dependency such as:

```text
example_container.a.update.complete
    ->
example_child.b.destroy.start
```

Another possibility would be an explicit operation dependency construct:

```hcl
operation_dependency {
  before = example_container.a.update
  after  = example_child.b.destroy
}
```

These examples are intended only to illustrate the required semantics, not to prescribe the eventual syntax.

### Consider both previous and desired relationships

Terraform should also consider dependency relationships that disappear during a transition.

Conceptually:

```text
G_previous = relationships before the change
G_desired  = relationships in desired configuration
Actions    = planned create/update/replace/destroy operations
```

The execution graph could then be constructed from:

```text
TransitionGraph(G_previous, G_desired, Actions)
```

rather than considering only relationships that remain present in the desired configuration.

For example, if:

```text
G_previous:

A -> B
```

becomes:

```text
G_desired:

A

B removed
```

and the planner determines:

```text
A = UPDATE
B = DESTROY
```

then the disappearing relationship between A and B is potentially significant to the transition and should remain available while constructing the operation graph.

It may not be safe to automatically infer the correct semantics from every disappearing dependency because different remote APIs have different lifecycle requirements. Therefore, explicit operation constraints and/or provider-supplied relationship semantics may also be required.

### Provider-declared lifecycle relationships

Longer term, the Terraform provider protocol could allow providers to supply lifecycle constraints associated with relationships enforced by remote APIs.

Conceptually:

```text
Relationship:
    source: A
    target: B

Lifecycle constraint:
    removal of the reference from A must complete
    before B can be destroyed
```

For example, an infrastructure provider could know that a particular relationship has the following semantics:

```text
A currently references B

Removing B requires:

A.update(remove B reference)
        ->
A.update.complete
        ->
B.destroy
```

Providers understand API-specific referential integrity constraints, while Terraform Core controls the global execution graph.

This suggests an architecture where providers can contribute operation constraints and Terraform Core incorporates those constraints into the final operation DAG.

### Preserve declarative semantics

This feature should not establish arbitrary procedural ordering of Terraform configuration.

Source-code order should remain irrelevant.

Instead:

```text
Configuration
      +
Previous relationships
      +
Desired relationships
      +
Provider lifecycle semantics
      |
      v
Planned operations
      |
      v
Operation dependency DAG
      |
      v
Single Terraform apply
```

The intent is to make Terraform's transition model more declarative, not less.

### Initial implementation scope

A useful first implementation could focus specifically on:

```text
resource A UPDATE
    ->
resource B DESTROY
```

This would address an existing class of failures without requiring Terraform to immediately expose every possible combination of operation-level dependencies.

### Acceptance criteria

A minimal test provider could expose:

```hcl
resource "test_container" "a" {
  references = var.enabled ? [test_child.b[0].id] : []
}

resource "test_child" "b" {
  count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0
}
```

With:

```hcl
enabled = true
```

the initial relationship contains:

```text
test_container.a -> test_child.b[0]
```

Changing to:

```hcl
enabled = false
```

produces:

```text
test_container.a       UPDATE
test_child.b[0]        DESTROY
```

Terraform should be able to guarantee the operation edge:

```text
test_container.a.update.complete
        ->
test_child.b[0].destroy.start
```

The test should verify that this dependency exists in the execution graph rather than relying on scheduling, reduced parallelism, or incidental execution order.

### Goal

The overall goal is to evolve Terraform's dependency model from only:

```text
resource dependency graph
```

toward:

```text
resource relationships
        +
planned lifecycle actions
        +
operation-specific constraints
        |
        v
operation dependency graph
```

This would allow Terraform to declaratively describe not only a valid desired state, but also the dependencies required to safely transition between valid states.

### References

Related Terraform Core issues:

- #25010 - Update dependency before destroy
- #31769 - Dependency/order-of-operations issue involving resources modified in place
- #32136 - Update dependency before destroy when no replacement is created
- #35881 - Incorrect resource graph/order of operations involving AWS ENI and security groups

Related AWS provider issues demonstrating the same class of API ordering constraint:

- hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws#34807 - CloudWatch Composite Alarm dependency/destruction ordering
- hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws#17601 - WAFv2 IP Set/WebACL dependency ordering
- hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws#40128 - Image Builder ResourceDependencyException

The common graph requirement across these reports is:

```text
dependent.update
    ->
dependency.destroy
```

rather than only a resource-level relationship:

```text
dependent
    ->
dependency
```

These issues demonstrate the same general transition-ordering problem across different resource types and APIs. The requested feature is intended to address that problem in Terraform Core rather than introduce resource-specific workarounds.
issues.title: Support operation-level dependency ordering for update-before-destroy transitions

issues.body:
## Terraform Version

Terraform Core `main` as reviewed on 2026-11-09. This is a feature request, not a bug report against a specific released binary.

## Use Cases

As a reusable module publisher, I want to understand adoption of my public Terraform Registry module across real Terraform runs, including whether module instances are newly created, subsequently applied, or deleted. The telemetry must be provider-agnostic and authored entirely in the packaged module, because module publishers cannot control consumers' CLI flags, wrappers, or provider choices.

For Azure Verified Modules (https://aka.ms/avm), a module may report selected adoption context such as tenant ID and subscription ID obtained from a provider data source. The consumer must be able to inspect and disable or redirect this behavior globally from the root configuration.

## Attempted Solutions

- Terraform Core's existing experimental OTLP trace exporter is opt-in and emits traces, but does not provide a stable, complete module-usage event or a module-authored data payload.
- A telemetry provider resource (for example, ModTM) can report module lifecycle data, but requires a provider and introduces a resource/data source into module configuration and the plan.
- Provider-defined functions are intended to be pure and side-effect-free; an unused function result is not a reliable lifecycle hook.
- Registry download counts are not a reliable measure of modules actually applied.

These approaches do not meet the combined requirements of packaged module declaration, provider independence, apply lifecycle semantics, and an out-of-band event.

## Proposal

>NOTE: If after any tweaks this proposal is accepted, the Microsoft team would be happy to contribute / collaborate on this feature.

Add a module-scoped `telemetry` block to Terraform Core. It declares an **OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) Logs export endpoint** and an optional map of additional telemetry data. Core derives module source and resolved version, associates a stable pseudonymous ID with each logical module instance, and sends an OTLP Logs record after a successful apply. This is not a resource or data source and must not represent an infrastructure change in the plan. 

**The endpoint must accept OpenTelemetry Protocol log exports (OTLP Logs); a generic HTTP webhook or vendor-specific non-OTLP ingestion endpoint is not sufficient.**

Example module configuration (illustrative syntax):

```hcl
telemetry {
  endpoint = "https://telemetry.publisher.example.com/v1/logs" # OTLP/HTTP Logs endpoint (illustrative)

  data = {
    tenant_id       = data.azapi_client_data.current.tenant_id
    subscription_id = data.azapi_client_data.current.subscription_id
  }
}
```

The block has no `enabled`, `count`, or `for_each`. Each module instance to which the declaration applies reports independently; nested modules with their own declaration report independently, and `count`/`for_each` instances receive distinct IDs.

### Root-level controls and source policy

Add a root-only `terraform` telemetry setting that controls all module telemetry, including nested modules. Illustrative syntax:

```hcl
terraform {
  telemetry {
    enabled            = false
    allow_non_registry = true
    endpoint           = "https://organization.example.com/v1/logs" # OTLP/HTTP Logs endpoint (illustrative)
  }
}
```

An environment variable provides the equivalent controls. Follow Terraform's normal precedence: an explicit root `terraform` setting wins over its equivalent environment variable; otherwise the environment variable wins over the default. Defaults are enabled, public Terraform Registry sources only, and no global endpoint override. A root OTLP Logs endpoint override replaces module-declared destinations globally; otherwise each module's OTLP Logs endpoint is used. Neither endpoint is a generic webhook. A child module cannot override root controls.

By default, emit only for modules resolved from the public Terraform Registry. Reporting for other sources is disabled unless the root opts in. When enabled for non-registry modules, report canonical source and ref/revision where available, removing embedded credentials.

### Event semantics

- Emit one event per telemetry-declared logical module instance per successful apply, including successful no-op applies. Do not emit on `init`, `plan`, or failed apply.
- Classify the module lifecycle as `created` on its first successful apply, `updated` on subsequent successful applies, and `deleted` when a successful apply removes the module instance from management/state and Core can reliably identify it from prior metadata. This classification is about the module instance, not individual resources in the module.
- Include an event ID and a stable pseudonymous module-instance correlation ID. Persist the latter across plans/applies for the same logical instance. Removed module calls use prior metadata for deletion where available; otherwise omit the event.
- Define behavior for full destroy, module source/version changes, `count`/`for_each` key changes, retries, duplicate delivery, and direct state operations. Do not claim exactly-once delivery.

### Plan and state

The plan must retain the telemetry declaration, endpoint selection, module correlation ID, and additional data points needed for post-apply export. Do not show the telemetry payload in the ordinary human-readable plan. Values should follow output-like planning semantics: known values are represented in the plan; values not known until apply resolve when their dependencies become known, and export waits for successful apply. A failed apply sends no event. Document that saved plan artifacts contain telemetry values and may be inspectable through machine-readable interfaces.

State must retain the correlation ID and the prior module identity/declaration/data needed to emit a deletion event after module removal. The exact internal encoding and migrations are implementation details, but state migration, compatibility, and cleanup behavior must be specified.

Illustrative OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) Logs record (exact OTLP schema/wire representation to be finalized):

```json
{
  "eventName": "terraform.module.usage",
  "timeUnixNano": "1794250000000000000",
  "attributes": {
    "event.id": "apply-event-uuid",
    "module.instance_id": "stable-pseudonymous-uuid",
    "module.source": "registry.terraform.io/contoso/avm-example/azurerm",
    "module.version": "1.2.3",
    "module.lifecycle.action": "updated",
    "terraform.operation": "apply",
    "module.telemetry.data.tenant_id": "tenant-id",
    "module.telemetry.data.subscription_id": "subscription-id"
  }
}
```

Illustrative state metadata (not a proposed public state format):

```json
{
  "terraform_telemetry": {
    "schema_version": 1,
    "module_instances": {
      "internal-module-instance-key": {
        "module_instance_id": "stable-pseudonymous-uuid",
        "source": "registry.terraform.io/contoso/avm-example/azurerm",
        "version": "1.2.3",
        "endpoint": "https://telemetry.publisher.example.com/v1/logs",
        "last_applied_data": {
          "tenant_id": "tenant-id",
          "subscription_id": "subscription-id"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Privacy, delivery, and security

Reject sensitive values in `data` unless explicitly declassified by module code, e.g. with `nonsensitive(...)`. Declassification is an explicit author decision, not a guarantee of safe disclosure. Document that payload values are stored in plan/state and sent to the configured endpoint.

Do not collect undeclared module inputs, resource addresses, or state contents. Require HTTPS and normal certificate validation. Version 1 does not support authentication to telemetry endpoints: module blocks and root endpoint overrides cannot configure credentials, tokens, or authentication headers. Future versions may add a secure authentication mechanism, particularly for customer-controlled collectors. Bound export time and make it best-effort: telemetry failure must not fail or materially delay the infrastructure apply. Specify payload-size/value-type limits and retry behavior.

### Compatibility

This requires Terraform Core and language changes. Older Terraform versions will reject the new block; define the minimum supporting version and behavior for compatible CLIs and remote execution environments that do not implement it. The feature should define a stable OTLP log schema rather than relying on the current experimental, trace-only Core exporter.
